This shows that his descendants have persisted and maintained a place of prestige in Israel until the time of the prophet Zechariah.
H5416G.origine: The name Nathan comes from the Hebrew natan, which means "to give" or "he who gives." It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing a quality or divine blessing. In this case, the context of birth — the son of a powerful king — gives the name a particular resonance: it is a "given" from God to King David.
H5416G.emploi: Nathan appears four times in the Bible: twice in the lists of David's sons in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:14 and 1 Chronicles 3:5 and 14:4), where he is presented as one of the four sons born to Bathsheba in Jerusalem. These three successive passages show that the ancient genealogies of Israel regarded him as an established figure of the royal lineage. Then, in Zechariah 12:12, written several centuries later, Nathan is cited as the ancestor of a house or clan that still persists and participates in the national mourning of the day of the Messiah. This last mention reveals that his lineage has maintained a lasting dynastic or social importance.
H5416G.portee: Nathan's presence in biblical genealogies, and particularly his mention in Zechariah 12:12 alongside the mourning of the pierced Messiah, shows how the Bible weaves the continuity of the messianic promise through generations. It is a reminder that God's salvation passes through concrete human lineages, and that even the distant descendants of great kings participate in the divine plan of salvation.

sens: The prophet of David and Solomon
The one who conveys God's word to the king
A man from Judah during the time of the united monarchy
H5416H.detail:
1. Nathan is primarily the prophet who lived at the court of King David around 1000 B.C. He intervenes at decisive moments in the monarchy of Israel: David confides his plan to build a temple to him (2 Samuel 7:2), and Nathan relays the words and vision that God gives him in response.

2. Nathan is the one who, speaking in the name of the Lord, denounces David's sin after the affair with Bathsheba. He tells the king a parable about a poor man and his lamb (2 Samuel 12:1-7), a story that leads David to acknowledge his wrongdoing. He is a courageous prophet who does not hesitate to correct the king himself.

3. Nathan also plays a crucial political role during Solomon's reign: he supports Solomon's anointing as king at Gihon (1 Kings 1:45), ensuring the continuity of David's dynasty. He stands alongside the priest Zadok and the mighty Benaiah, among the loyal followers of King David.
H5416H.origine: The name Nathan means "giver" or "he has given" in Hebrew. The prophet bears a name that suits his mission: he is the one who gives God's word to the king and to Israel. Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament, including a son of David born of Bathsheba (2 Samuel 12:25), but the most notable Nathan is this court prophet, a major figure during the time of David and Solomon.
H5416H.emploi: Nathan appears thirty times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the books of Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles. He is first presented as "the prophet" to David (2 Samuel 7:2-4), tasked with conveying the king's plans regarding the temple of the Lord. His prophetic role is affirmed when he intervenes in the succession crisis: he is a loyal ally of Solomon against Adonijah (1 Kings 1). Chronicles mentions him alongside other prophets who recorded royal history. Nathan embodies the court prophet: he does not flatter power, as he reprimands David, but he supports God's plan for the monarchy.
H5416H.portee: Nathan shows the Christian reader that true prophecy is never servile before power. A true prophet tells the truth to the king when the king is wrong, as Nathan did after David's sin. His story also teaches that God guides the history of Israel through his prophets, even in the most political times. For those who read these accounts, Nathan reminds us that seeking God and listening to his word is the path to royal wisdom.

sens: man from Zobah, father of a warrior of David
brother of Joel
H5416I.detail:
1. Nathan is a man from Zobah (a region in Syria). His son Jigal was among David's renowned warriors (2 Samuel 23:36), indicating that Nathan came from a family of good social standing.
2. Nathan is also mentioned as the brother of Joel (1 Chronicles 11:38). Joel himself served David and was listed among his most esteemed warriors.
H5416I.origine: The name Nathan means "he has given" or "giver" in Hebrew, derived from a root expressing giving or donation. It is a theophoric name, attributing the action of giving to God, very common in biblical families to express gratitude toward the Lord.
H5416I.emploi: Nathan appears twice in the preserved biblical texts, always in the lists of David's warriors. He is not the prophet Nathan known during the reign of David and Solomon, nor one of the other Nathans mentioned elsewhere in Scripture. This man from Zobah simply represents a military officer from the time of King David, identified by his place of origin and his familial connection to Joel.

sens: Son of Attai and father of Zabad, from the tribe of Judah
H5416J.detail: Nathan is a man from the tribe of Judah mentioned in the genealogy of Attai. He is the father of Zabad and occupies a place in the genealogical lineage of the people of Judah during the period of the divided monarchy, as indicated in 1 Chronicles 2:36.
H5416J.origine: The name Nathan means "the one who gives" or "giver" in Hebrew, derived from the root נתן (natan) which means "to give." It is a common name in the Old Testament, borne by several distinct characters. The genealogical passage in 1 Chronicles clearly identifies him: it is Nathan son of Attai and father of Zabad.
H5416J.emploi: Nathan is a name borne by nine different people in the Old Testament. This one, mentioned in 1 Chronicles 2:36, belongs to the tribe of Judah and appears in a genealogical list established during the period of the divided monarchy. He represents a link in the genealogical chain of God's people and bears witness to the continuity of family lines in Israel.

sens: Leader of a family of Israel returned from exile in Babylon
Man who returned from captivity with Ezra
H5416K.detail: 1. Nathan is a leader among the Israelite families who left Babylon to return to Jerusalem during the return from exile, around the 5th century B.C. His name, which means "giver" or "the one who gives," is a common theophoric name in Israel. 2. He is mentioned in Ezra 8:16 among the leaders who were summoned to prepare the return journey with Ezra: he was one of the responsible men organizing the return of the exiles to the land of Israel.
H5416K.origine: The name Nathan comes from the Hebrew verb נָתַן (natan), which means "to give." It is a theophoric name, meaning it expresses a relationship to God: "God gives" or simply "giver." This same verb has produced other names in Israel (like Nathanael, "God has given"). The name conveys the idea of generosity and divine giving.
H5416K.emploi: Nathan appears only once in the Segond translations: in Ezra 8:16, during the return from exile in Babylon under Ezra's leadership. He is presented there as one of the leaders specifically called to guide the return of the Israelite families. His appearance in this historical and official context indicates that he was a person of responsibility and authority among the returned exiles.

sens: Man of the time of exile and return
Giver (the one who gives)
H5416L.detail: Nathan is a Hebrew proper name that literally means "the one who gives" or "giver." Although the term designates several different characters in the Bible — including the famous prophet during the time of David and Solomon, and a son of David born of Bathsheba — in this passage from Ezra 10:39, it refers to a man living at the time of the exile and return, mentioned only once among the men who had taken foreign wives and who were to send them away. This Nathan is known to us only through this single verse and plays no significant role in the biblical narrative.
H5416L.origine: The name Nathan comes from the Hebrew root נתן (natan), which means "to give." It is a participle that expresses the one who gives or who is in the habit of giving. This theophoric name (containing the idea of God) suggests a relationship to generosity or divine providence. The same root appears in many biblical names and in the common usage of the verb "to give" throughout Scripture.
H5416L.emploi: The name Nathan appears several times in the Bible designating different people at different times. In this specific passage from Ezra 10:39, it refers to a man from the time of the return from exile under Ezra, at the moment when the Israelites returned from Babylon had to separate from the foreign wives they had married in violation of the Law. This is the only mention of this particular Nathan in the Scriptures. Other characters bearing the same name — notably the prophet Nathan under David and the son of David — play much more significant roles elsewhere in the Bible, but this one remains a minor figure in the narrative of restoration after the exile.

sens: Leader of the tribe of Issachar at the time of the Exodus
Son of Zuar
H5417G.detail: Nethaneel is a military and tribal leader chosen to represent the sons of Issachar during the census of the people of Israel at the foot of Sinai. He appears in the lists of tribal leaders and participates in the organization of the camp of the people (Numbers 1:8; 2:5). He is also the second to present the Lord's consecration offering, providing animals and goods for the newly established sanctuary (Numbers 7:18, 23). At the departure from the desert, he commands the army (or the body) of his tribe (Numbers 10:15). He is a trustworthy man, chosen for these major responsibilities.
H5417G.origine: The name "Nethaneel" means "God has given" or "given of God" in Hebrew: it combines "Nethan" (given, from the verb "to give") and "El" (God). This theophoric name expresses the faith that God granted this son as a gift to his father Zuar. This name reflects a common religious conviction in Israel: to recognize that every gift, especially children, comes from the hand of God.
H5417G.emploi: Nethaneel is mentioned five times in the book of Numbers, always in the context of the census and organization of the people at Sinai. He is presented as prince or leader of his tribe (Numbers 1:8; 2:5), a title that confers recognized authority. His role in the consecration offerings (Numbers 7) shows that he represents not only his tribe militarily but also religiously. The order of presentation (he is the second) suggests a certain preeminence. He finally intervenes in the organization of the people's march toward the Promised Land (Numbers 10:15). These concentrated references in Numbers highlight his importance during the formation of the people.
H5417G.portee: Nethaneel embodies the responsibility of leading a people in the service of God. His selection by God shows that it is not always the greatest or most famous who receive important charges: it is faithfulness and the ability to serve that matter. His commitment to ritual offerings reminds us that every true leader first recognizes divine sovereignty. For the believer, Nethaneel is a discreet model of service to the people of God.

sens: Son of Jesse and brother of David
H5417H.detail: Nethaneel is a son of Jesse, the father of David, mentioned in the genealogy of Jesse's children in 1 Chronicles 2:14, where he is named as the fourth son. He belongs to the tribe of Judah and lived during the time of the united monarchy in Israel.
H5417H.origine: The name Nethaneel means "given of God" in Hebrew: it is composed of "nethan" (given) and "El" (God). This name expresses the belief that this child was a gift from God to his family.
H5417H.emploi: Nethaneel appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:14, in the genealogical list of Jesse's eight sons. He is presented as the fourth son, between Abinadab and Raddaï. He is therefore the brother of King David. The Bible reports nothing else about his life or actions.

sens: Priest during the time of King David
The one who sounds the trumpet before the ark
Son of a priestly family
Representative of temple service
H5417I.detail:
1. Nethaneel is a priest who serves under the reign of King David. In 1 Chronicles 15:24, he appears among the priests assigned a solemn role.
2. His main action is to sound the trumpet before the ark of God when it is transported. This is not a simple musical task: it is an act of worship that accompanies the moment when the ark, the symbol of God's presence, is brought to Jerusalem — a major event in Israel's history under David.
3. His name means "given of God," which reflects a common belief in the faith of Israel: children are a gift from the Lord. This name was perfectly suited for a servant of the temple.
H5417I.origine: The name Nethaneel is composed of two Hebrew elements: "natan" (to give) and "el" (God). It is a theophoric name, meaning it incorporates the divine name, as many Israelite names do. This type of name expressed the people's trust that God gives and provides for all needs. In the Hebrew Old Testament, several men bear this name at different periods of Israel's history.
H5417I.emploi: Although the name Nethaneel is borne by several characters in the Old Testament (leaders, priests, Levites at various times in Israel's history), the one mentioned here in our provided usage is a priest under David, an actor in the worship in Jerusalem. His role as trumpet-sounder places him among the servants of the sanctuary. He represents the liturgical function of the priests who assisted the king in the great religious ceremonies of the united kingdom.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi, father of the scribe Schemaeja
Name meaning 'given of God'
H5417J.detail:
1. Nethaneel is a Levite mentioned in 1 Chronicles 24:6 as the father of Schemaeja, the scribe who recorded the names of the priests and Levites during the drawing of lots that King David had ordered. This drawing organized the priestly families for temple service.
2. His Hebrew name literally means "given of God": it expresses the recognition that this child is a gift from God. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, reflecting faith in divine generosity.
H5417J.origine: The name Nethaneel is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Natan," which means "to give," and "El," which designates God. This construction reflects the piety of the parents who recognize in the birth of their son a divine gift. Many characters bore this name at different periods in Israel, making it a very popular name in biblical tradition.
H5417J.emploi: Nethaneel appears only once in the Bible in the provided usages, in 1 Chronicles 24:6. He is identified there as the father of Schemaeja, a royal officer who assisted King David and the priests in recording the decisions of the drawing of lots among the priestly families. This recording was an important task in organizing the temple worship. Although Nethaneel himself does not perform the reported action, his mention underscores the importance of his family in the religious and administrative structures of the kingdom of Judah.
H5417J.portee: This character reminds us that the tasks of organizing worship and service to God required trustworthy men from Levitical families. His name, "given of God," invites the reader to see in every person that God places in our lives a precious gift, especially those who help us serve in the church and community.

sens: Son of Obed-Edom, Levite during the time of the united monarchy
Name meaning 'given of God'
H5417K.detail: Nethaneel is a proper name designating a Levite, son of Obed-Edom, mentioned only once in the Bible in 1 Chronicles 26:4. He was the fifth son of Obed-Edom, who was a musician and gatekeeper of the sanctuary during the time of King David. His name carries the meaning of "given of God," reminding that this child was perceived as a divine gift to his family.
H5417K.origine: The name Nethaneel is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Nathan" (to give) and "El" (God). It literally means "God has given" or "given of God." This type of theophoric name was common in Israel to express gratitude to God or the assurance that the child was a divine gift. It is a name that reflects the faith of the Hebrew people in God's providence over families.
H5417K.emploi: Nethaneel is mentioned only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 26:4, where he appears in the list of the sons of Obed-Edom. Obed-Edom was an important figure during David's time, serving as a gatekeeper and musician of the tabernacle. Nethaneel, being the fifth son, was part of this family of sanctuary servants. This brief mention shows that even the secondary figures of the Old Testament belonged to families dedicated to the service of God.
H5417K.portee: This name reminds us that in the life of God's people, every person, even obscure in the eyes of the world, has a place in the divine plan. Nethaneel, though little known, came from a family dedicated to the service of the Temple, illustrating how God builds a faithful community generation after generation. His name also evokes the trust that Hebrew parents placed in God, recognizing each child as a precious gift.

sens: Prince de Juda envoyé en mission par le roi Jehoshaphat
H5417L.detail: 1. Nethaneel est un prince de Juda qui a vécu sous le règne du roi Jehoshaphat (IXe siècle avant J.-C.). Avec d'autres chefs, il a été envoyé par le roi parcourir les villes du royaume pour y enseigner la Loi divine aux habitants (2 Chroniques 17:7). C'était une initiative royale pour instruire le peuple dans les voies de Dieu.
H5417L.origine: Le nom Nethaneel signifie « donné de Dieu » en hébreu : il est composé de deux éléments, « natan » (donner) et « El » (Dieu). Ce nom exprime la conviction que cet enfant était un don de Dieu à ses parents. Plusieurs hommes portaient ce nom dans l'Ancien Testament, à différentes périodes — certains à l'époque de l'exode, d'autres à l'époque du roi David, d'autres encore à celle d'Esdras ou de Néhémie.
H5417L.emploi: Nethaneel est mentionné une seule fois dans la Bible, en 2 Chroniques 17:7, comme l'un des chefs envoyés en mission officielle par le roi Jehoshaphat. Son rôle était d'enseigner la Loi de l'Éternel dans les villes de Juda. Son apparition dans ce contexte souligne l'importance que le roi attachait à la formation religieuse du peuple et le rôle des chefs lévites et civils dans cette mission d'instruction.

sens: Chef lévite au temps du roi Josias de Juda
H5417M.detail: Nethaneel est un chef des Lévites qui, sous le règne de Josias, contribue généreusement à la célébration de la Pâque en donnant des agneaux et des bœufs pour le sacrifice (2 Chroniques 35:9). Il apparaît aux côtés de ses frères Conania et Schemaeja, tous trois responsables des Lévites et tous trois impliqués dans l'organisation des offrandes festives.
H5417M.origine: Le nom Nethaneel signifie « donné de Dieu » en hébreu. Il provient de la racine « natan » (donner) et du nom divin « El » (Dieu). Ce nom célèbre la générosité divine et la confiance en Dieu. Plusieurs autres personnages du même nom apparaissent dans la Bible à des périodes différentes, notamment un chef de la tribu d'Issacar à l'Exode et un frère de David.
H5417M.emploi: Nethaneel est mentionné une seule fois dans la Bible, en 2 Chroniques 35:9, au moment où le roi Josias organise une grande célébration de la Pâque. Il est présenté comme un des chefs des Lévites, aux côtés de ses frères Conania et Schemaeja. Tous trois se distinguent par leur générosité en fournissant des sacrifices abondants : cinq mille agneaux et cinq cents bœufs pour la fête. Ce rôle montre que les Lévites jouaient un rôle d'organisation et de direction religieuse importante pendant les grandes fêtes du culte juif.
H5417M.portee: Ce passage souligne l'importance de la générosité et du service envers Dieu dans le culte. Nethaneel et ses frères donnent de façon abondante pour honorer Dieu lors de la Pâque, montrant que le leadership religieux vrai s'exprime par le don de soi et le soutien des célébrations de la foi communautaire.

sens: Un prêtre de la famille de Paschhur à l'époque d'Esdras
H5417N.detail: 1. Nethaneel est un prêtre appartenant à la famille sacerdotale de Paschhur, mentionné une seule fois dans la Bible au moment du retour d'exil après la captivité de Babylone. Son nom signifie « donné de Dieu » en hébreu. À cette époque, le peuple d'Israël revient à Jérusalem et réorganise le culte du temple ; Nethaneel figure parmi les prêtres qui, comme beaucoup d'autres, avaient pris des femmes étrangères (non israélites) et durent s'en séparer pour respecter la pureté de la communauté du retour (Esdras 10:22).
H5417N.origine: Le nom Nethaneel vient de l'hébreu « Nathan » (donné) et « El » (Dieu), littéralement « donné de Dieu ». C'est un théophore, un nom qui exprime la confiance envers Dieu. L'Ancien Testament connaît plusieurs porteurs de ce nom à différentes périodes — un chef de la tribu d'Issacar au Sinaï, un fils de Jessé frère de David, des lévites du temps de David et de Josias — mais celui-ci est spécifiquement un prêtre du temps du retour d'exil.
H5417N.emploi: Nethaneel n'apparaît qu'une fois dans la Bible, en Esdras 10:22. Il est cité dans le contexte du retour d'exil, au moment où Esdras prend des mesures strictes pour restaurer la pureté du culte après la captivité babylonienne. Le texte mentionne que plusieurs prêtres de la famille de Paschhur, dont Nethaneel, avaient épousé des femmes étrangères, ce qui était considéré comme contraire à la loi et à l'alliance. Nethaneel représente ainsi l'un des nombreux membres du peuple d'Israël qui ont dû corriger cette situation en se séparant de leurs femmes étrangères pour se conformer aux exigences de la restauration religieuse post-exilique.

sens: Prêtre de la famille sacerdotale de Jédaja au temps du retour d'exil
H5417O.detail: 1. Nethaneel est un prêtre qui représente la famille de Jédaja à l'époque où Jérusalem se reconstruit après l'exil à Babylone. Son nom figure dans la liste des prêtres et des Lévites revenus avec Zorobabel (Néhémie 12:21).
H5417O.origine: Le nom signifie « donné de Dieu » en hébreu : il combine deux mots, « natan » (donner) et « El » (Dieu). Ce nom exprime la foi que cet enfant était un don divin à ses parents. Plusieurs personnages bibliques portent ce nom à différentes périodes — un chef au moment de l'exode, un fils de Jessé, des prêtres sous David — mais celui mentionné en Néhémie est une figure du retour d'exil.
H5417O.emploi: Nethaneel apparaît une seule fois dans la Bible, en Néhémie 12:21, où il est cité comme le représentant de la famille sacerdotale de Jédaja sous le grand prêtre Jéhoïakim. C'est une mention brève dans le contexte administratif et généalogique de la reconstruction du Temple et du culte à Jérusalem après le retour de captivité.

sens: Lévite de la tribu de Lévi, musicien au temps de Néhémie
Homme appartenant à la famille d'Asaph
Participant à la dédicace du mur de Jérusalem
H5417P.detail:
1. Nethaneel est un Lévite, c'est-à-dire un membre de la tribu de Lévi consacrée au service du temple. Son nom apparaît dans le récit de la dédicace du mur de Jérusalem, après le retour de l'exil (Néhémie 12:36).
2. Il appartient à la famille d'Asaph, une lignée de musiciens et de chantres du temple. Ces familles étaient responsables de la musique et des chants durant les cérémonies religieuses.
3. Nethaneel joue des instruments de musique lors de la célébration solennelle de l'achèvement du mur de Jérusalem, aux côtés de ses frères et d'autres Lévites, avec les instruments traditionnels de David (Néhémie 12:36).
H5417P.origine: Le nom « Nethaneel » signifie « donné de Dieu » en hébreu, composé de « nathan » (donner) et « el » (Dieu). C'est un nom théophore courant en Israël, exprimant l'idée que l'enfant est un don de la divinité. Plusieurs personnages portent ce nom dans l'Ancien Testament, depuis l'époque de l'exode jusqu'à celle du retour de Babylonie.
H5417P.emploi: Nethaneel apparaît une seule fois dans la Bible française (Néhémie 12:36), lors de la narration de la cérémonie de dédicace du mur de Jérusalem, peu après le retour d'exil (vers 445 avant J.-C.). Il est présenté comme l'un des Lévites musiciens qui jouent des instruments lors de cette procession solennelle, aux côtés de ses frères Schemaeja, Azareel, Milalaï, Guilalaï, Maaï, Juda et Hanani. Son mention parmi ces noms confirme son rôle important dans la vie religieuse de la communauté restaurée. Bien que la Segond 1910 ne le mentionne qu'une fois, d'autres traditions rabbiniques associent le nom Nethaneel à plusieurs autres personnages importants de l'histoire d'Israël, notamment un chef d'Issachar au temps de l'exode et un fils de Jesse (frère de David).

sens: son of Elishama, from the royal family of Judah, whose son Ishmael assassinated Gedaliah
father of Jehudi
father of Johanan and other children
Levite, one of the four sons of Asaph the musician
Levite during the time of King Jehoshaphat of Judah
H5418G.detail:
1. Nethania is a member of the royal family of Judah, son of Elishama. His son Ishmael, contrary to promises, assassinated the governor Gedaliah whom Nebuchadnezzar had established (Jeremiah 41:2). This crime brings chaos after the fall of Jerusalem.
2. The name Nethania also refers to the father of Jehudi, an officer of King Jehoiakim (mentioned in the references of tradition).
3. The same name is held by a Levite, one of the four sons of the musician Asaph during the time of David and the temple.
4. A Levite of the same name also served during the time of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, in liturgical or administrative functions.
H5418G.origine: The name Nethania means "given by Jehovah" ("nethan" = given, and "yahu" = Jehovah). It expresses the belief that this child was a gift from the Lord to his family. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, built on the same root as the verb "natan" (to give).
H5418G.emploi: Nethania appears sixteen times in the Bible, mainly in the account of the fall of Jerusalem and the events that followed (2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 40-41). The main Nethania known is the father of Ishmael, whose horrific crime of treachery—the assassination of Gedaliah and the massacre of his companions—marks the last days of the kingdom of Judah. Other lesser-known Nethania bear the same name during the royal and Levitical periods, showing that it was a respected name in influential families.
H5418G.portee: The story of Nethania and his son Ishmael reminds us that even a noble genealogy and a promising name do not guarantee faithfulness. The assassination of Gedaliah by Ishmael, son of Nethania, closes the door to the last chances of reconstruction and peace in Judah. This account teaches that iniquity can emerge from the highest families, and that personal choices weigh more than inherited honor.

sens: A Levite, musician of the temple during the reign of King David
H5418H.detail: 1. Nethania is a Levite, meaning a member of the tribe of Levi dedicated to the service of the temple. He is one of the four sons of the musician Asaph, a famous royal choir master. Along with his brothers Zaccur, Joseph, and Asahiah, he leads a musical ensemble in the temple and participates in the liturgy of worship (1 Chronicles 25:2). His name means "given by the Lord," reflecting gratitude to God for the birth of a son.
H5418H.origine: The name Nethania comes from two Hebrew elements: "ne­than" (to give) and "yah" (abbreviation of the divine name Yahweh, the Lord). It thus means "given by the Lord" or "the Lord has given." This formation is typical of theophoric Hebrew names, which celebrate an act or attribute of God.
H5418H.emploi: Nethania is mentioned twice in 1 Chronicles 25, at the heart of the list of musicians and choir leaders of the temple. In 1 Chronicles 25:2, he is presented as the son of Asaph and is among the four sons who prophesied in music under the king's orders. In 1 Chronicles 25:12, he is named again during the assignment of service rotations in the temple: "the fifth, to Nethania, his sons and his brothers, twelve." These two verses place him in the context of the religious organization under David and confirm his role as a musical family leader in the service of worship.

sens: Levite sent by King Jehoshaphat to teach the Law in the cities of Judah
H5418I.detail: Nethania is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when King Jehoshaphat of Judah organizes a religious teaching mission. The king sends several Levites and priests to travel through the cities of Judah to teach the Law to the people (2 Chronicles 17:8). Nethania is part of this group of temple servants tasked with instructing the Israelites.
H5418I.origine: The name Nethania means "given by the Lord" in Hebrew: it comes from the root "natan" (to give) and the divine name "Yah" (God). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God, expressing the parents' gratitude for this son received as a divine gift. Several men bore this name in Israel's history.
H5418I.emploi: Nethania appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 17:8, where he is designated as one of the Levites that King Jehoshaphat sent to teach the Law in the cities of Judah. This context shows an important moment in the history of the Judean monarchy: the king sought to strengthen the people's faith by organizing religious missions. The mention of Nethania among this group highlights the role of the Levites in the spiritual education of Israel.

sens: man of Judah during the divided monarchy
father of Jehudi
H5418J.detail:
1. Nethania is a man living at the time of the division of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah. He is mentioned as the father of Jehudi, who was sent by the leaders of Judah to bring the prophet Baruch and ask him to read the book of the prophet Jeremiah before them (Jeremiah 36:14).
2. His role in biblical history is limited to this familial link: he is known only through his son Jehudi, who played a role in the transmission of the prophetic message.
H5418J.origine: The name Nethania means "given by the Lord" or "the Lord has given." It is composed of the Hebrew word "natan" (to give) and the divine name "Yah" (the Lord). This type of theophoric name, which includes the name of God, was common in Israel to express gratitude to the Lord or to entrust the child to His protection.
H5418J.emploi: Nethania appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 36:14, where he is presented as the father of Jehudi, son of Shelemiah and grandson of Cushai. It is in the dramatic context of the scroll of Jeremiah: after the prophet had his words written down by Baruch, the leaders of Judah sent Jehudi, a descendant of Nethania, to summon Baruch and invite him to read this prophetic scroll. Although Nethania himself is not an actor in the narrative, his lineage ties him to the major events preceding the fall of Jerusalem.

sens: Officer of Judah during the reign of King Josiah
H5419.detail: Nathan-Melech is an official in the service of King Josiah, mentioned only once in the Bible during major religious reforms. His name literally means "gift of the king" or "don of the king," suggesting his importance at court (2 Kings 23:11).
H5419.origine: The name Nathan-Melech is composed of two Hebrew elements: Nathan means "he has given" or "gift" (root נתן), and Melech means "king." Together, it expresses the idea of a person designated or elevated by the king, a name borne by a figure of royal prestige.
H5419.emploi: Nathan-Melech appears only once in Scripture, in 2 Kings 23:11, in the context of the great religious reforms carried out by King Josiah. It is learned that he was an officer or chamberlain of the king, responsible for managing buildings or royal objects related to the worship of the sun. Josiah, in purifying the temple and the worship of Judah, also ordered the removal of the horses that previous kings had dedicated to the sun and which were located near the residence of Nathan-Melech.

sens: Demolish, break, reduce to ruins
Annihilate someone's path, block their way
H5420.detail:
1. The verb literally means to break or demolish a structure, to reduce it to nothing. In Job 30:13, Job says that his enemies "destroy" his path — they do not merely strike him, they are intent on ruining the road he takes, the image of a life or project that is completely sabotaged.
2. In a broader figurative sense, it means to annihilate something established or important for someone — here the "path" represents Job's life, dignity, or direction. The enemies leave nothing standing.
H5420.origine: The Hebrew root natsas evokes the idea of breaking, shattering, or forcefully demolishing. It appears rarely in the Old Testament, making each occurrence significant. The word paints a concrete image of deliberate and systematic destruction.
H5420.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 30:13. Job, in the midst of his suffering, lists how his enemies persecute him: they strike him, spit on him, and worse — they "destroy" his path. This context shows that the word expresses not only physical violence but also the malicious intent to nullify someone's life or future.
H5420.portee: This word helps the reader measure the depth of Job's suffering. His enemies do not settle for fleeting attacks: they systematically destroy his path, his future, his integrity. For any believer facing hostility, it is a reminder that God sees these destructions and that, like Job, one can cry out to God.

sens: To be broken, destroyed, annihilated
To lose strength, effectiveness, or power
H5421.detail:
1. The word denotes the action of breaking or destroying something solid, reducing it to pieces or severely damaging it. In Job 4:10, the teeth of young lions are "broken," meaning shattered, losing their ability to bite and threaten.
2. Figuratively, to break means to annihilate, to destroy the power or strength of something. When a lion's teeth are broken, the lion itself is defeated, rendered harmless — it is all its weapon, its instrument of domination, that is destroyed.
H5421.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that evokes the idea of breaking or fracturing. The form we encounter (niphal) is passive: it describes the state of something that has been broken, that undergoes the action of breaking. This verb belongs to the family of terms that express physical destruction or loss of effectiveness.
H5421.emploi: The word appears only once in the received biblical text. It is used in Bildad's speech to Job, in a poetic context: Bildad contrasts the end of the roaring of powerful lions with the destruction of their teeth. It is an image of the fall of one who seemed invincible, an illustration that even apparent strength eventually collapses. The passage uses the language of animal nature to speak of divine judgment on the proud.
H5421.portee: For the reader, this image of broken teeth reminds us that all earthly power and weapons of domination are fragile before God. It is a call not to fear those who seem strong: the Lord has the power to nullify the strength of those who oppose Him. This word comforts the oppressed and warns those who trust in their own power.

sens: Demolish or destroy a building, an altar, a wall
Break or shatter an object
Overthrow a person, defeat or bring them down
Figuratively, annihilate a plan, a work, a kingdom
H5422.detail:
1. Demolish or destroy a building: the verb evokes the action of throwing down, breaking a built structure. Exodus 34:13 commands the Israelites to overthrow the altars of the pagan nations; Judges 9:45 reports that Abimelech razed a city, which means to completely destroy it by throwing it to the ground.

2. Break or shatter an object: the word also applies to the destruction of objects or body parts. In Job 19:10, Job says that God has "overthrown" all his plans, like breaking a barrier or a dam that collapses.

3. Overthrow a person or bring them down: figuratively, to overthrow someone means to knock them down, to defeat them. Jeremiah 1:10 uses this verb for the prophetic work of destruction: "overthrow the kingdoms".

4. Figuratively, annihilate, ruin: the verb denotes the collapse of a work, a plan, or a power. This is the broadest sense: to overthrow means to bring down what was elevated, to reduce to nothing what seemed stable.
H5422.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the idea of tearing, pulling towards oneself to break. The verb appears in several forms in Hebrew (Qal, Niphal, Piel, Pual, Hophal) which nuance the action: pulling down, breaking oneself or being broken, accomplishing a deliberate destruction. The basic image is that of the violent gesture of one who seizes an object and throws it to the ground to destroy it.
H5422.emploi: This verb appears 41 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical and prophetic narratives. It is first used for religious reforms: overthrowing the altars and idols of false gods (Exodus 34:13; 2 Chronicles 34:7). It also describes military sieges and destructions of cities and walls (Judges 9:45; Jeremiah 39:8; 52:14). The prophets use it to announce divine judgment: Jeremiah receives the command to overthrow the nations (Jeremiah 1:10; 18:7; 31:28). The meaning varies little: it is always a deliberate and violent destruction, a bringing down of what was established.
H5422.portee: This verb reveals the gravity of divine judgment and spiritual warfare. Overthrowing the altars of idols expresses zeal for the worship of the true God and the rejection of false gods. For the believer, the word reminds us that God has the absolute power to overthrow what opposes His kingdom, and that He calls His people to destroy within themselves what distances them from Him. It is also a word of deliverance: God can break the chains of evil that ensnare us.

sens: To pull, detach, or violently separate something from its point of attachment
To break or shatter something that holds, binds, or ties
To remove, extract, or withdraw abruptly
To detach, break, or separate (passive sense)
H5423.detail:
1. To pull, detach, or violently separate something from its point of attachment: the word describes the action of grasping and pulling forcefully to separate one thing from another. In Leviticus 22:24, it refers to testicles "torn away" from the animal. It is a forced and complete separation.

2. To break or shatter something that holds, binds, or ties: the word applies to bonds, ropes, chains that are broken or shattered. In Psalm 2:3, the people cry, "Let us break their bonds" — they break the chains that bind. In Jeremiah 30:8, the Lord "will break your bonds".

3. To remove, extract, or withdraw abruptly: it can refer to pulling something out of a place or situation. In Isaiah 33:20, the cords of the tent will not be "detached" — nothing will tear away the stability of Jerusalem.

4. To detach, break, or separate (passive sense): the thing itself breaks or separates. In Jeremiah 6:29, "the dross does not detach" from the lead during refining — it refuses to separate from the metal.
H5423.origine: The Hebrew verb nataq comes from a root that evokes the action of pulling, separating, breaking. The basic image is that of a force that tears away, detaching one thing from another. The root is used in several forms (Qal, Niphal, Piel, Hiphil) to nuance the idea: to tear away oneself, to be torn away, to tear away completely or violently, to cause to be torn away. The verb appears 26 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the prophetic and historical books.
H5423.emploi: Nataq is used to describe the action of tearing away, breaking, or detaching in very varied contexts. It can refer to tearing away limbs (Leviticus 22:24), breaking bonds or chains (Psalms 2:3, Jeremiah 30:8), detaching cords or stakes (Isaiah 33:20), or separating dross from molten metal (Jeremiah 6:29). The word is also used in the sense of "to divert, to draw away" (Judges 20:31: the Benjamites "drew away from the city"). It is a very concrete word, describing a violent or at least energetic physical action. Depending on the context and the form of the verb used, the emphasis is either on the one who tears away or on what is torn away and separates.
H5423.portee: This word reminds the believer that only God can break the bonds that chain him — whether it be sin, oppression, or fear. When the Bible says that the Lord "will break" our bonds, it assures a radical and energetic deliverance. Conversely, when it describes what tears or detaches, it evokes the fragility of everything that is not founded on God: human alliances, the forces of enemies, the structures of evil. It is a word of liberation and divine power.

sens: Contagious skin affliction, probably a form of leprosy or fungal disease of the scalp and beard
State of legal impurity declared by the priest after examination
Sign of violation of ritual purity that only water and time can erase
H5424.detail:
1. Scab is a skin disease that primarily affects the scalp and beard. The Hebrew word refers to a contagious skin affliction characterized by a rash and the loss of yellowish or abnormal hair (Leviticus 13:30: the priest examines whether the hair is "yellowish and thin"). It is one of the recognized variants of leprosy by the Law.

2. In the eyes of the Law of Israel, scab renders a person legally impure and they must be isolated from worship and the community. The priest conducts a careful examination to determine if it is indeed scab: he observes whether the wound is deeper than the skin, whether the hair has changed color, and he may examine it several times over seven days (Leviticus 13:31-34). If all signs of contagion disappear, the priest declares them pure.

3. A person can be declared impure for a confirmed scab, then re-examined and recognized as healed — which shows that impurity is not permanent, unlike severe leprosy. Leviticus 13:34 shows that after washing clothes and the disappearance of signs, the person "will be pure". It is a "minor" impurity that can resolve through time and hygiene, under the priest's control.
H5424.origine: The Hebrew word "neteq" (נֶתֶק) comes from a root that evokes tearing away or removal — the idea that this disease "tears away" or causes hair to fall out. This root emphasizes the visible symptom that characterizes the disease: hair loss and the resulting partial baldness. The word belongs to the family of terms designating contagious skin diseases in the Levitical Law.
H5424.emploi: The word "scab" (neteq) appears nine times in Hebrew, all in Leviticus chapters 13 and 14, which list the diseases declared impure by the Law. Scab is presented there as a specific affliction of the scalp or beard, distinguished from other forms of leprosy by its location and examination signs (hair color, depth of the wound). Unlike leprosy, which spreads and persists, scab can disappear after a few days of isolation and shaving: the priest re-examines it on the seventh day and can declare the person pure if it has not worsened (Leviticus 13:32-34). This distinction shows that the Law recognizes degrees in disease and impurity, and that it allows for healing and restoration.
H5424.portee: Scab teaches the reader that ritual impurity is not a definitive condemnation: it can be examined, mitigated, and erased. It also shows that God entrusts the priest, a figure of wisdom and judgment, with the responsibility to discern the pure from the impure in concrete and progressive situations. For the believer today, this disease serves as a reminder that healing takes time, humility before established authority, and trust that God can restore one who has fallen.

sens: To move suddenly from one place to another by a springing motion of the body
To make a leap, a jump
To vibrate, tremble violently
To cause a sudden movement or jolt
H5425A.detail: 1. The primary meaning is to launch oneself suddenly from one place to another: it is the quick and lively movement of a creature that leaps. The locusts mentioned in Leviticus have legs "above their feet, to leap on the earth" — it is their natural ability to spring (Leviticus 11:21). 2. The word also describes the heart that leaps, that "springs" from its place under emotion or fear: Job says that his heart "leaps out of its place", an image of the physical panic caused by a terrifying sight (Job 37:1). 3. In a figurative or intensive sense, the word expresses a violent jolt, a tremor: to make the nations "tremble" is to shake them by a manifestation of divine power (Habakkuk 3:6). The violent springing motion extends into a movement that shakes, that stirs.
H5425A.origine: The verb natar comes from a root that evokes sudden and lively movement: a rebound, a quick spring. The root is related to the physical idea of jumping or shivering. In biblical Hebrew, it appears in this limited number of contexts, but its basic image — a push, a surge — remains constant. It is akin to words that express sudden and involuntary movements of the body.
H5425A.emploi: The verb natar appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always to describe a quick and sudden movement. In Leviticus 11:21, it refers to the natural jump of a locust — an ordinary animal act. In Job 37:1, it becomes the symbol of the heart that panics under religious fear, vibrating with emotion. In Habakkuk 3:6, it expresses the divine power that makes tremble: God "makes the nations tremble", and this trembling extends even to the eternal mountains. The word thus progresses from the concrete (the jump of an insect) to the spiritual (the cosmic shaking caused by God).
H5425A.portee: This word reminds us of God's formidable sovereignty: making nations tremble with a single glance shows His absolute power. It also invites the believer to recognize that all creation obeys His command and that nothing escapes His domain. It is a word of reverence and assurance for one who knows that their God masters all things.

sens: To detach, undo a physical link or attachment
To free someone from chains or captivity
To release, let go
To liberate from oppression or servitude
H5425B.detail:
1. In a literal sense, the word means to undo a knot or detach a rope, as one would unbind someone's tied hands. In Psalms 105:20, the king "removes the bonds" of the prisoner Joseph: it is to concretely detach the chains that bind him.
2. By extension, it means to free someone who is chained or imprisoned. The Lord "delivers the captives" (Psalms 146:7), meaning He unbinds those who are held in slavery and restores them to freedom.
3. The word can also describe the act of letting go, releasing a grip or hold. In Job 6:9, Job asks God to "stretch out" His hand — here, it is to release the hand, to loosen it so that it strikes him mortally.
4. Figuratively, it expresses the idea of liberating from a moral and spiritual domination or oppression. In Isaiah 58:6, "to loose the bonds of wickedness" means to free the oppressed from the injustice that crushes them.
H5425B.origine: The Hebrew verb natar comes from a root that evokes the idea of loosening, undoing. The Semitic language often uses the image of a bond or rope to speak of what holds, oppresses, or binds. The related Aramaic expresses more the idea of stripping away or peeling off. This word belongs to the family of liberation verbs that run throughout the Bible, alongside others that mean "to break," "to shatter," or "to free."
H5425B.emploi: This verb appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in Psalms and Isaiah. It is first used for physical liberation: removing the chains of a prisoner (Psalms 105:20) or the bonds of captivity (Isaiah 58:6). It can also express a violent gesture or release: in Job 6:9, Job asks God to "let go" of His hand to finish him off. In all cases, the word refers to the action of granting freedom or ceasing a constraint — whether physical or spiritual. It is a word of deliverance, at the very heart of the expectations of the oppressed people.
H5425B.portee: This word speaks to those who suffer under a weight, an injustice, or guilt. It reminds that God is the one who unbinds, who frees the captives and releases the oppressed. For the believer, it is a promise: prayer and waiting on God can bring freedom where chains reign. It is also a call to unbind those who are bound by injustice and wickedness.

sens: To make something fall by abrupt and repeated movements
To remove or disperse by shaking
To drive away, to chase off
H5426.detail:
1. To shake means to make something fall by abrupt and repeated movements, as one would shake a garment to remove dust. In King Nebuchadnezzar's dream, the angel commands to "shake" the foliage of the immense tree to disperse its fruits (Daniel 4:14).
2. The word evokes the action of stripping or laying bare through movement: shaking the foliage causes the fruits and leaves to fall, reducing the tree to its bare trunk. It is an image of denuding and destruction.
3. By extension, to shake also means to drive away or make depart: it is the effect of these violent movements — animals flee from under the tree that is being shaken.
H5426.origine: The Hebrew word natar comes from a root that evokes the idea of stripping away or removing. The form used here (aphel) gives the verb a causative sense: "to make removed," "to make fall." The connection with Greek and other ancient languages suggests a family of words expressing the action of shaking or stripping away.
H5426.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 4:14. It is used in the context of Nebuchadnezzar's prophetic dream: an angel cries out the command to cut down a great tree, to cut off its branches, and to shake its foliage to disperse the fruits. This image symbolizes the impending fall of the king — the tree represents his kingdom and power, and shaking it announces his deposition.
H5426.portee: This word illustrates how the images of the divine dream express, in concrete and vivid language, God's judgments upon the powerful. Shaking the tree shows that human power, even vast and imposing, can be brought to nothing by the hand of God. For the reader, it serves as a reminder that no one can stand before God's judgment.

sens: White, crystalline mineral substance, natural or produced, used for cleaning and laundry
Image of purity and effectiveness in washing
Biblical symbol of the ineffectiveness of human efforts in the face of spiritual guilt
H5427.detail:
1. Nitre is a white, alkaline powder that was found naturally in Egypt and the Middle East. It was mainly used for washing, degreasing fabrics, and cleansing the skin. It was a luxury product, effective and highly valued. Jeremiah 2:22 mentions it as a powerful cleaning agent: "Though you wash yourself with nitre…"
2. The Bible uses nitre as an image: its rapid and visible action in water (it foams and reacts) makes it a symbol of lively reaction, striking effectiveness. In Proverbs 25:20, pouring vinegar on nitre creates an effervescence: it is an image of violent contrast, like singing joyfully in front of someone who is suffering.
3. In spiritual language, nitre becomes the symbol of what is insufficient: even with nitre, the dirtiest skin cannot truly be purified; likewise, no human effort can erase sin before God. Jeremiah 2:22 clearly expresses this: "Your iniquity would remain marked before me," despite all the nitre in the world.
H5427.origine: The Hebrew word נֶתֶר (neter) designates this well-known alkaline substance in ancient Egypt. Its exact origin is debated, but it may come from the Egyptian word that referred to this powder. In Greek, the Septuagint translates this word as νίτρον (nitron), from which we get the French "natron." It is a word that designates a concrete and material reality, very familiar to the Eastern readers of the biblical text.
H5427.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, only in Proverbs and Jeremiah, at times when it is necessary to speak of cleansing. In Proverbs 25:20, nitre is mentioned for its striking chemical action: pouring vinegar on it (two acidic and basic substances) creates a violent reaction — an image of the ridiculous effect of joy in the face of sadness. In Jeremiah 2:22, the prophet uses nitre as the best possible cleaning agent to contrast with the impossibility of purifying Judah from its sin: even what cleans best is not enough. These two uses play on the known reality of nitre to build strong images.
H5427.portee: Nitre teaches the reader a spiritual truth that runs throughout the Bible: no human force or resource, no matter how powerful, can purify the soul from sin and guilt. Only God can truly wash and restore. It is a lesson in humility and an invitation to seek purification in Him, not in our own efforts. This word invites us to recognize our limits and the grace of God.

sens: Remove or detach something by pulling hard
Destroy, overturn a building or a city
Annihilate a people, evict them from their land
Dry up, interrupt the natural course of something
H5428.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to remove something by pulling it forcefully, as one tears a plant from the ground. Jeremiah 1:10 speaks of Ezekiel who would tear away nations, an image of the prophet who destroys by his word.
2. By extension, it means to overturn, demolish human constructions. Psalms 9:7 states that God has "overturned" enemy cities, destroying them down to their foundations.
3. The word also applies to expulsion: God tears His people from their land, evicting and scattering them. Deuteronomy 29:28 describes how the Lord tore Israel from its land in anger and cast it into another.
4. Finally, it can describe the interruption of a natural process: Jeremiah 18:14 asks if the waters that flow from Lebanon can dry up, meaning to be torn from their source and cease to flow.
H5428.origine: The Hebrew verb נָתַשׁ (natash) primarily evokes the violent action of pulling, tearing away. It is a verb of physical action that has gained figurative meanings: what was an action on plants (to tear them away) has extended to buildings (to overturn them), to peoples (to exile them), and to natural processes (to interrupt them). The root expresses a destructive force that separates, that removes definitively.
H5428.emploi: The verb natash appears 19 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the writings of the prophets Jeremiah (who uses it 11 times) and in historical books. God is the almost exclusive subject: He tears away, overturns, destroys what opposes Him or disobeys. But the word can also refer to what God spares or restores: after having torn Israel away, He will tear it away again from deportation and bring it back (Jeremiah 12:15). The context alternates between destruction and restoration, showing that "to tear away" is an act of divine power that can serve both judgment and mercy.
H5428.portee: This word teaches the reader that God has absolute power over nations and peoples: He can establish or overturn them according to His will and justice. But it also invites hope: the tearing away is never final. God who tears away in judgment can replant in grace. It is a word of assurance for the people of God: He alone holds the power of life and death over empires and human plans.

sens: Unit of capacity for measuring grains or flour
Quantity that a standard measuring container can hold
Price or value of a certain quantity of food
H5429.detail:
1. The measure (seah) is a concrete unit for evaluating grains or flour: Abraham asks for "three measures of fine flour" (Genesis 18:6) to prepare a meal, showing that flour is counted by distinct measures, just as it is counted today by kilograms.
2. It is also the capacity of a defined container or space: Elijah builds an altar with a trench "of the capacity of two measures of seed" (1 Kings 18:32), meaning large enough to sow that amount of grain.
3. In pricing contexts, the measure becomes a commercial unit: during the lifted famine, "a measure of fine flour will be for a shekel" (2 Kings 7:1), illustrating the relationship between a fixed quantity and its cost.
H5429.origine: The word seah comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of pouring or measuring by pouring. It is a technical term from ancient agriculture and commerce, used to quantify cereals, the main food wealth of biblical societies. This measure had a recognized standard value: it represented about a third of an ephah, a larger measure.
H5429.emploi: This word appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in narratives from the Old Testament. It mainly appears in domestic or commercial scenes: Abraham requests it to make cakes (Genesis 18:6), Abigail offers it as a gift (1 Samuel 25:18). It also appears in prophecies about the price of food during famine (2 Kings 7:1, 7:16, 7:18), where the measure becomes the standard of value. Each use reinforces the idea of a recognized and reliable unit for food commerce.
H5429.portee: This word reminds us that in antiquity, as today, food was a concrete and measurable concern. The measure also symbolizes the generosity of Abraham and Abigail: they give a precise and generous quantity. In famine prophecies, it shows how God controls even markets and prices, and how His word is fulfilled down to the last detail.

sens: Soldier's or warrior's shoe
Garment destroyed by fire after victory
H5430.detail:
1. The word designates a shoe worn by soldiers in battle, particularly the reinforced boots or sandals that a warrior wears for combat. It is an element of military gear, mentioned alongside blood-stained war garments (Isaiah 9:4).
2. By extension, the shoe represents here the warrior's equipment intended to be burned after victory: the prophetic context of Isaiah 9:4 announces the destruction of war materials in flames, symbolizing the definitive end of conflict and the peace that follows.
H5430.origine: The Hebrew word seon designates the footgear of the combatant. It belongs to the vocabulary of war and armament. The term evokes the concrete image of military footwear, worn by walking and battle, a tangible and earthly object whose final combustion is announced in the Bible.
H5430.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 9:4, in a prophetic passage where Isaiah describes the messianic end of war. The shoe is mentioned in the plural as part of the warrior's equipment alongside blood-stained garments, both destined to be consumed by fire. This unique occurrence fits into a vision of hope: the destruction of war tools symbolizes the triumph of peace and the establishment of Christ's reign.
H5430.portee: This word reminds us that war and its instruments are temporary and destined to disappear. For the believer, the prophecy of Isaiah 9:4 speaks of Christian hope: the sword and the combat shoe will be burned when true justice and peace reign in Christ. It is an invitation not to place trust in the weapons of this world, but in the eternal victory of the Lord.

sens: Walk on something by putting the weight of one's body on it
Trample or crush by walking
Wear (shoes, clothing) by putting it on oneself
H5431.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of walking on something, placing one's weight on it: to tread the earth, to tread a path. This is the primary physical meaning of the word.
2. By extension, it can mean to trample or crush underfoot what one treads: the image of an army treading the ground as they march, or crushing their enemies.
3. In Isaiah 9:4, the word takes on the meaning of "to wear" or "to have on oneself": the warrior shoe that one treads, meaning that one wears on their feet in battle. This is a particular usage where to tread means to have on the body.
H5431.origine: The Hebrew verb סָאַן comes from a root that expresses the physical action of walking by pressing the weight of the body, hence the image of treading, of trampling. The family of this word overlaps with terms related to walking and the weight of the body on the ground. It is an uncommon word that retains its concrete and bodily flavor.
H5431.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 9:4. It is used there to describe the war shoes that soldiers wear (tread) in battle. The context is one of messianic peace vision: the weapons and garments of war, including the shoes worn on the feet, will be burned. The word emphasizes the physical and bodily nature: one treads, one wears, one walks in these combat gear.
H5431.portee: This word reminds us that the peace of the Messiah will involve the disappearance of weapons and war garments. In reading it, the believer understands that the salvation brought by Christ is not only spiritual: it also transforms the physical reality of the world, even to the warrior's shoes. It is an invitation to hope for true and complete peace.

sens: Action of moderating, proportioning something with prudence
Limitation, restriction imposed on an action or punishment
Quantity or degree appropriate to an end
H5432.detail:
1. The verb conveys the idea of an action carried out "with measure," meaning in a moderate and controlled manner, without excess. In Isaiah 27:8, God punishes His people through exile, but He does so "with measure": He does not completely destroy them; He moderates the severity of His judgment. The image is that of a hand that restrains its strength so as not to strike beyond what is necessary.
2. "Measure" stands in opposition to excess and limitless vengeance. It represents a just proportion between sin and sanction, between fault and punishment. By acting this way, God demonstrates His justice: He punishes, but not blindly. This limitation of punishment also reveals His mercy.
H5432.origine: This Hebrew verb belongs to a family of words that express the idea of moderation and proportion. The form used here (an intensive form of the verb) emphasizes the action of restraining, mastering, not allowing to overflow. The root evokes the image of measuring or holding something back to keep it within appropriate limits.
H5432.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 27:8. It describes how God treats Israel during its exile: He punishes, indeed, but by restraining His hand, measuring His judgment. This passage reveals that even in divine correction, there is justice and restraint, not unbridled cruelty. The exile itself, though painful, is an act of measured discipline.
H5432.portee: This word reminds the believer that God never acts with excess, even when He punishes. Divine judgment is always just and proportionate, never tyrannical or excessively cruel. For the Christian, this invites imitation of this fair justice: to correct without vengeance, to discipline without cruelty, and to see in God a judge who tempers His rigor with wisdom.

sens: to absorb a beverage in large quantities
to consume alcohol excessively or habitually
to be drunk or soaked in alcohol
H5433A.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is simply to drink a lot: to absorb a large quantity of liquid, especially wine or strong drinks. It is the physical action of drinking abundantly (Isaiah 56:12: "we will drink strong drinks").
2. The word takes on a moral hue when it designates someone who habitually indulges in this excess: a drinker or a drunkard, a person whose character trait is to drink too much. Proverbs 23:20-21 warns against the company of wine drinkers, for the drunkard becomes impoverished.
3. By extension, the word describes the state of someone who is drunk: soaked in alcohol to the point of losing reason. Nahum 1:10 compares enemies to people drunk on their wine, unable to resist.
H5433A.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the action of drinking, with the idea of doing so abundantly, without restraint. The word belongs to the family of verbs related to consumption and drunkenness. In Hebrew, this root emphasizes less the simple act of drinking than the excess and intemperance that result from it.
H5433A.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts of warning or moral criticism. Proverbs uses it to designate the drinker (one who abuses wine) and the drunkard, emphasizing the consequences: impoverishment and shame. Isaiah places it in the mouth of one who boasts of drinking incessantly. Nahum uses it poetically to evoke the spiritual drunkenness and blindness of God's enemies. The word always carries a negative connotation.
H5433A.portee: This word reminds us of the biblical teaching on temperance and the danger of intemperance. The Bible does not condemn wine in itself but warns against its abuse: excess leads to ruin, loss of dignity, and distancing from wisdom. It is an invitation to self-control and vigilance.

sens: excessive and habitual consumption of alcohol
the state of chronic drunkenness
the habit of drinking excessively
H5433B.detail:
1. Drunkenness refers to the act of regularly drinking too much wine, leading to intoxication. In Deuteronomy 21:20, a rebellious son is described as indulging in drunkenness: he visibly abuses wine, recognized by the entire community.
2. It is a habitual state, not a mere temporary drunkenness. The word evokes someone who identifies by their excessive love of alcohol and whose vice characterizes their behavior.
3. Drunkenness appears as a serious moral failing, ranked alongside insubordination and rebellion: it shows that a person has turned away from righteousness and lost self-control.
H5433B.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be intoxicated" or "to be drunk." The original meaning is that of intoxication by alcohol. In biblical Hebrew, this term first designates the action or state of drunkenness, then the chronic habit of drinking excessively—drunkenness as an established vice.
H5433B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Segond translations, in Deuteronomy 21:20, in the law concerning the rebellious son. It is a grave term: it shows that drunkenness is mentioned among the most serious faults of a child, alongside insubordination and rebellion. The context is legal and moral, emphasizing that alcoholism was considered a destructive vice threatening family and community order.
H5433B.portee: Drunkenness is presented in the Bible as a serious vice that destroys the person and the household. This word reminds the reader that self-control, even in the use of things that are good in themselves like wine, is a sign of wisdom and fear of God. For a believer, it is a call to temperance and vigilance against passions that enslave.

sens: son of Cush, ancestor of the peoples of Arabia and North-East Africa
nation or region south of Palestine, probably in Ethiopia
H5434G.detail:
1. Saba is primarily a figure from ancient times, son of Cush. In the genealogy of nations following the Flood, he appears alongside his brothers Havilah, Sabta, Raamah, and Sabtechah (Genesis 10:7 and 1 Chronicles 1:9). This name designates a founding ancestor of a people, from whom the Sabeans will descend.
2. By extension, the name Saba designates the people or region he founded, located south of the Promised Land, probably in Ethiopia or in Southern Arabia. It is from this people that an important commercial civilization of the ancient Near East developed.
H5434G.origine: The name Saba literally means "wood of wine" or could also be translated as "the one who drinks" according to some etymologies. It appears as a genealogical proper name, typical of the ancient peoples' tables of the Near East. The same root appears in geographical and personal names related to the kingdoms of the south and southeast of the Mediterranean.
H5434G.emploi: Saba appears only twice in the canonical Bible, both in genealogical lists: in Genesis 10:7 and in 1 Chronicles 1:9. These two references are parallel and describe the descendants of Cush after the Flood. Saba is presented as the son of Cush and brother of the founders of other important peoples. Later in biblical history, the people of the Sabeans (notably the Queen of Sheba) will play a significant commercial role, although Saba himself is mentioned only in these ancient genealogies.

sens: Region or ancient kingdom located south of Palestine, probably in Ethiopia
H5434H.detail: Saba refers to a people and territory in the south of Palestine, often identified with Ethiopia or South Arabia. It is a nation known for its wealth and power, capable of offering tributes and valuable gifts. In Psalm 72:10, the kings of Saba are among the rulers who bring tributes to the king of Israel in a vision of prosperity and universal dominion. In Isaiah 43:3, Saba is mentioned alongside Egypt and Ethiopia, symbolizing the distant nations that God is willing to give up to redeem His people Israel — an act demonstrating God's surpassing love for His chosen ones.
H5434H.origine: The name Saba (Hebrew סְבָא) literally means "wood" or evokes the idea of "drink." This region was known in antiquity as a prosperous trading center, the seat of a powerful kingdom. It likely corresponds to the territory of ancient Yemen or the Horn of Africa, in the area that the ancients called Happy Arabia or Ethiopia.
H5434H.emploi: Saba appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible (Psalms 72:10 and Isaiah 43:3). In both cases, it is mentioned in connection with other great powers or distant regions — Tarshish, Egypt, Ethiopia. These mentions reflect the prestige and remoteness of this kingdom in the eyes of Israel. The poetic and prophetic context shows that Saba represents the wealth of the known world and its subjugation to the God of Israel.
H5434H.portee: These passages remind God's people that all kingdoms and riches of the earth are under divine sovereignty. The mention of Saba alongside powerful nations invites recognition that God governs all nations according to His love for His chosen people.

sens: alcoholic beverage made from fermented grapes
the act of drinking wine or an alcoholic beverage
state of drunkenness or intoxication from alcohol
H5435.detail: 1. Wine is the beverage obtained by fermenting grape juice: it is the most common alcoholic drink in the biblical Middle East. In Isaiah 1:22, wine was mixed with water to dilute it, which was a normal practice; here, God denounces a watered-down or poor-quality wine as an image of the corruption of the people. 2. The word also refers to the act of drinking, consuming wine or an alcoholic beverage. In Hosea 4:18, the people "cease to drink" to engage in prostitution, showing how the text uses this term to speak of the act of consumption. 3. By extension, wine evokes the state of drunkenness or intoxication: in Nahum 1:10, the enemies are described as "drunk on their wine," an image of confusion and loss of control before their destruction.
H5435.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that refers to the idea of mixing or fermentation. Wine was central to the daily and religious life of Israel: it was used in meals, festivals, and temple sacrifices. Biblical Hebrew has several terms for wine depending on its state or use, but this is one of the most common.
H5435.emploi: This word appears 3 times in the provided passages. In Isaiah 1:22, it symbolizes the moral degeneration of the people through the image of watered-down wine. In Hosea 4:18, it simply denotes the act of drinking, opposed to prostitution as a sign of debauchery. In Nahum 1:10, drunkenness is an image of disorientation and helplessness in the face of God's judgment. In all cases, wine refers either to a legitimate pleasure that has become corrupted or to an intoxication that removes clarity.
H5435.portee: Wine in the Bible is neither condemned nor glorified in itself: it is a gift from God that can be received with gratitude or misused through excess. These verses remind us that drunkenness, a symbol of loss of self-control, is incompatible with wisdom and obedience to God. For the believer, it is an invitation to sobriety of mind and vigilance.

sens: People of South Arabia, merchants and warriors
Inhabitants of the region of Saba, descendants of Sheba
H5436.detail:
1. The Sabians are an ancient people of South Arabia, known for being prosperous merchants and warriors. The Bible mentions them particularly in contexts of wealth and power: in Isaiah 45:14, the prophet announces that the gains of Egypt, the profits of Ethiopia, and the riches of the Sabians will pass into the hands of God's people and they will walk in His footsteps.
2. In Ezekiel 23:42, the Sabians appear as men coming from the desert who bring precious bracelets and sumptuous crowns, thus highlighting the luxury and splendor associated with this trading people.
H5436.origine: The name Sabians comes from Sheba (שְׁבָא), a figure mentioned in Genesis 10:7 as the son of Raamah and brother of Dedan, himself a descendant of Cush. This name designates the people and region of Saba, an ancient kingdom of South Arabia famous for its trade routes, incense, and precious stones. The name carries the idea of wealth and distinction related to distant commerce.
H5436.emploi: The term "Sabians" appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, each time in a prophetic context speaking of wealth and splendor. In Isaiah 45:14, Cyrus is presented as the one before whom nations come with their tributes, including the Sabians with their precious goods. In Ezekiel 23:42, the Sabians come from the desert to bring luxurious ornaments. In both cases, the Sabians embody the prosperity and power of the distant kingdoms of Arabia.
H5436.portee: The Sabians remind the reader that the God of Israel reigns over all peoples, even the most powerful and richest. Seeing the wealth of the Sabians come to Jerusalem or serve God's plan expresses the universal sovereignty of the Lord and the certainty that all nations, in their glory, are subject to His will.

sens: To perform a circular or rotational movement around an axis or a central point
To go around something, to circumvent or encircle it
To change direction, to turn away or return on one's path
To bring something or someone back to a place or person
To transform or change nature
To completely envelop or surround
H5437I.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a turning or rotating movement: to pivot, to turn around an axis. This is the simplest image of the verb, the physical movement that everyone knows.

2. This rotation can encompass a space: to walk around something, to circumvent it, to encircle it. Thus, one "turns around" a city to besiege it (Joshua 6).

3. To turn can also mean to change direction, to stray from the straight path or to return to it: the idea of a diversion or a return.

4. By extension, "to bring back" means to turn something towards a place or person — the movement that draws closer. In 1 Chronicles 13:3, David says, "Let us bring the ark of our God back to us": it is about turning the ark towards the people.

5. To turn can also transform or change: to change a state into another, to "turn" something into its opposite.

6. The verb can describe an envelope, a closure: to completely surround, to go around to enclose or protect.
H5437I.origine: This Hebrew verb primarily expresses the concrete image of rotational or circular movement, from which all figurative meanings derive. The common root across several forms of the verb (Qal, Niphal, Piel, Hiphil) shows how central this image of turning and rotation is in Hebrew to express change, return, closeness, and transformation. The French "tourner" captures its essence: the movement that changes perspective and orientation.
H5437I.emploi: This verb appears twice in the provided passages. In 1 Chronicles 13:3, it is used to describe the action of "bringing back" the divine ark to the people: it is a directed action, a movement that turns something towards a destination. In Psalms 71:21, the same verb expresses a moral or spiritual transformation: the idea that God "increases" comfort, or "turns" the heart towards joy. The context shows that the verb is used for both physical movements and for inner changes or emotional returns.
H5437I.portee: This verb invites the reader to meditate on change: it reminds us that God can turn our hearts, "bring back" what was far away, transform our spiritual direction. The heart that turns away from evil "turns" towards God. It is also a word of hope: what has "turned" away can "turn" back towards us.

sens: To turn, to change direction
To go around, to circumvent, to encircle
To divert from, to distance, to repel
To pass to someone else, to transfer
H5437J.detail:
1. The primary meaning is movement: to turn or change orientation. It is the image of a person or thing pivoting, changing course (Jeremiah 21:4: the Lord turns away the weapons of war, meaning he directs them elsewhere).
2. From this comes the idea of circumventing or encircling: to go around something, to surround it. This applies to marching around a city or the action of a troop encircling a position.
3. To turn away also means to dismiss, to repel, to distance oneself. It is to push away something that bothers or troubles you: "Turn your eyes away from me" (Song of Solomon 6:5), meaning to remove them, to turn them elsewhere.
4. Finally, the word can mean to transfer, to pass to someone else: "Their houses will pass to others" (Jeremiah 6:12), meaning they will be turned away from their current owners and entrusted to others.
H5437J.origine: The Hebrew root sabab first evokes circular movement, the idea of turning around. It belongs to a family of words that all describe movements or changes in orientation. The basic image is that of turning, of rotation: something or someone changing direction or going around something.
H5437J.emploi: The verb sabab appears three times in the provided usages, always in a context of movement or transformation. In Song of Solomon 6:5, it means to repel or dismiss (to turn away the eyes). In Jeremiah 6:12, it expresses a change of ownership (houses passing to others). In Jeremiah 21:4, it describes the turning of a weapon or intention: the Lord turns away the weapons of war, he directs them in another direction. The word can thus describe a physical movement, a gesture of distancing, or a change of possession.
H5437J.portee: This word reminds us that God controls direction and the course of events. When the Lord "turns away" the weapons of war (Jeremiah 21:4), he shows that human plans are not beyond his control: he can redirect them, turn them around. For the believer, this also speaks of God's power to transform circumstances and to reorient what seemed impossible to stop.

sens: To turn, to pivot, to direct from one side to the other
To modify, to transform, to give a different turn
To replace someone or something with another
H5437K.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to turn or pivot in a direction, to go around, to circle something. It is like making a U-turn or walking around an object.

2. By extension, the word means to modify, to transform, to give a new turn to something that exists. In 2 Samuel 14:20, Joab sought to "change" the course of events, meaning to orient them differently.

3. In personal or political contexts, it means to replace, to substitute one person or thing for another. Pharaoh Necho "changed" the name of Eliakim to Jehoiakim (2 Kings 23:34), and the king of Babylon "changed" the name of Mattaniah to Zedekiah (2 Kings 24:17). This is a change of identity imposed by one authority upon another.
H5437K.origine: The Hebrew word סָבַב comes from a root that evokes the idea of turning, going around, circumventing. The root is very ancient and common in Semitic languages. Words from the same family denote a turn, a circle, a circuit.
