The basic image — turning around — has naturally extended to the meaning of modifying, since transforming something means moving it from one state to another.
H5437K.emploi: The verb סָבַב appears four times in the provided usages, all in a political or administrative context. In 2 Samuel 14:20, it describes Joab's action of seeking to "change" the outcome of events. But it is especially in the books of Kings and Chronicles that the meaning becomes very clear: it concerns the change of name imposed by a foreign authority on a defeated king. Pharaoh Necho "changes" the name of Eliakim (2 Kings 23:34 and 2 Chronicles 36:4), and the king of Babylon "changes" that of Mattaniah (2 Kings 24:17). These name changes symbolize the takeover and domination of the one who imposes this new name. The context shows that changing a name means changing identity and asserting authority.
H5437K.portee: This word reminds us that our identities and destinies are not definitive — they can be transformed. For the biblical reader, this raises a question: who has the right to change our name, our identity? The Bible suggests that only God can truly do this. Abram becomes Abraham, Sarai becomes Sarah, Saul becomes Paul. This divine name change is a mark of grace and covenant, not oppression. In contrast, when a foreign king changes the name of a defeated king, it marks servitude.

sens: Change, turnaround, turning of circumstances
Course, direction, orientation that events take
H5438.detail:
1. The word denotes a turning point, a moment when things change direction or shift unexpectedly. In 1 Kings 12:15, King Rehoboam refuses to listen to the people; this refusal is not a mere accident: it is a "turning point" ordained by God Himself, who thus redirects the course of events to fulfill His promise.
2. More broadly, it refers to how events unfold and develop, the direction a story takes. The turning point can be a critical moment where everything shifts.
H5438.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means to turn or change direction. It evokes the concrete image of something that turns or deviates from its path. The family of the word includes terms related to turning, rotation, or changing course.
H5438.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Kings 12:15. It is a rare but significant term: it describes the decisive moment when God diverts King Rehoboam's intention so that his actions serve the divine plan. The context shows that this "turning point" is not the work of chance, but of God's providence.
H5438.portee: This word reminds us that God controls even the turning points of history that seem most human, most political. When circumstances shifted and Rehoboam listened to his pride rather than wisdom, God directed this turning point toward the fulfillment of His word. This invites the believer to see God's hand behind the major turns in their own life.

sens: That surrounds, encircles, in a circle or on all sides
The space, the region, the immediate surroundings of a place or a person
Everything that surrounds, that is found on each side without exception
The limit, the border, the perimeter of an object
H5439G.detail:
1. This word primarily describes what surrounds something by forming a circle or occupying all sides at once. In Genesis 35:5, the terror of God spreads over "the cities that surrounded them," meaning the cities located in a circle around where Jacob was.
2. It also designates the immediate surroundings, the nearby region: in Numbers 16:27, Dathan and Abiram stand at the entrance of their tents "on all sides," meaning the people withdraw from all sides that surround them.
3. The word can emphasize the absence of exception — absolutely everywhere around: in Ezekiel 40:5, a wall "surrounded the house on all sides." 
4. Finally, it can simply refer to the perimeter or border of an object: in 1 Kings 7:24, gourds "surrounded" the edge of a large basin, forming its decoration all around.
H5439G.origine: This word comes from a root that evokes the idea of turning, going around. It is related to the image of the circle and circular movement. In Hebrew, it can be used as a noun (an enclosed place, a circuit), as an adverb (turning around, on all sides), or as a preposition (around). It is a very common word, especially in descriptive and architectural texts of the Bible.
H5439G.emploi: This word appears more than 230 times in the Old Testament, particularly in the historical and legislative books. It is frequently found in Exodus to describe the arrangements of the tabernacle and its furnishings (borders, edges, enclosures). It also appears in the architectural descriptions of kings (the temple of Solomon in 1 Kings 7) and in the Psalms to express a state of siege or encirclement. The context varies depending on whether it is a protection (the people surrounded by divine terror), a structure (walls and ornaments), or a threat (enemies attacking from all sides).
H5439G.portee: This word helps us recognize how the Bible describes divine protection or the danger that surrounds God's people. Seeing "around" reminds us that God knows everything that surrounds His people and can act from all sides at once. It is also an image of totality: when something "surrounds" on all sides, nothing is left to chance, which emphasizes God's enveloping presence or, conversely, the gravity of a threat.

sens: The places, regions, spaces that surround something or someone
The action of going around or circling around a point
From all sides, without exception, coming from any direction
H5439H.detail:
1. The places that surround: the word designates the spaces, the areas that encircle a place or an object. For example, in Exodus 7:24, the Egyptians dig "in the vicinity of the river" to find water, meaning in the surrounding areas, in the adjacent regions.

2. In circuit or around: the idea of traversing a boundary, going around. When blood is poured "all around" the altar in Leviticus 3:8 and 9:18, it is spread over the entire circumference, from end to end of the perimeter.

3. From all sides: the word expresses the idea that something comes, occurs, or threatens from all directions at once. In 1 Samuel 14:47, Saul makes war "on all sides" against his enemies, meaning he fights everywhere around him, on all fronts. Similarly, in Jeremiah 51:2, enemies "attack from all sides" against Babylon, assaulting from all directions.
H5439H.origine: The Hebrew word סָבִיב (saviv) comes from the root סבב (savav), which means "to turn around, to surround." This root paints the concrete image of something that turns, that forms a circle. The word thus primarily denotes the spatial dimension of circular movement or the environment that encircles. It is found in related words that express similar ideas: what surrounds, what is peripheral.
H5439H.emploi: The word appears 42 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of the Law (Exodus, Leviticus), in historical narratives (Samuel, Kings), and in the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel). It is used in three ways: first to describe the places bordering a space (the surroundings of a river), then to talk about actions that occur "all around" a central object, such as the pouring of blood "all around" the altar in sacrifices, and finally to express that something comes from "all sides" or "from all directions," indicating a convergence, an encirclement, or an omnipresence. This last nuance is very common in Jeremiah and Ezekiel to evoke the threats looming over Jerusalem or Babylon.
H5439H.portee: This word invites the reader to perceive God as the one who surrounds and protects His people (as in Job 1:10, where God has "put a hedge around" Job and his possessions), but also to recognize the omnipresence of danger or divine judgment that threatens "from all sides." It reminds us that nothing can escape God's attention or action.

sens: What surrounds a place, a person, or a thing on all sides
The space that extends around something
To announce or proclaim from one place to another
Every side, every direction
H5439I.detail:
1. What surrounds a place, a person, or a thing on all sides: the word primarily refers to the spaces, regions, or things that surround something on one side and the other. In Genesis 23:17, it refers to "all the trees that are in the field and in all its borders around" — meaning everywhere around the field of Ephron.
2. The space that extends around something in all directions: this is the notion of a complete circuit, a region that extends in a circle around a center. In Numbers 32:33, Moses distributes to the tribes "the land with its cities, with the territories of the cities of the land all around," meaning the entire region that surrounds these cities.
3. To announce or proclaim from one place to another, from all sides: the meaning shifts towards the idea of spreading news everywhere, making it known in all places. When the Philistines "proclaim" the victory in 1 Samuel 31:9, it literally means to shout it from all sides, to spread it throughout the land.
4. Every side, every direction together: the word can also express the idea of protection or coverage coming from everywhere at once. In 2 Chronicles 14:6, the Lord gives rest "from all sides" — meaning from every direction, without threat from anywhere.
H5439I.origine: The Hebrew word סָבִיב (saviv) comes from a root that means "to turn" or "to go around." It is related to the verb סָבַב (savav), which means "to go around, surround, turn." The basic image is that of circular movement, of going around something or someone. This root is common in biblical Hebrew to express the idea of encirclement, proximity in all directions.
H5439I.emploi: This word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible translated by Segond. It is primarily used to describe what surrounds a space or an object: the boundaries and territories around a property (Genesis 23:17, Numbers 32:33, Ezekiel 45:1), or to reinforce the idea of totality ("from all sides" in 2 Chronicles 14:6). It also takes on the meaning of "to proclaim" or "announce everywhere" in the context of the news that the Philistines spread (1 Samuel 31:9, 1 Chronicles 10:9), where the idea of "making known from everywhere" replaces that of "spatially surrounding." The word thus shows how the same root can express both spatial surrounding and the diffusion of information.
H5439I.portee: This word reminds the reader that nothing escapes observation: what surrounds a place is part of its integrity. It also expresses the biblical idea that God's protection or blessing can come "from all sides" — not just from one place, but completely. Finally, its use for "announcing everywhere" shows that good or bad news spreads quickly, from one end of the land to the other.

sens: Around something, in a circle
The space or places that surround a location
The people, the nations that are near and around
Everything that surrounds on all sides
H5439J.detail:
1. The word first describes what is around something, forming a closed circle: in Ezekiel 28:24-26, the enemies who "surround" Israel are the neighboring peoples who encircle and threaten it from all sides.
2. It also designates the region, the circuit, or the entirety of places located around a central point: it is the surrounding territory, the immediate proximity.
3. The word can also refer to surrounding people or nations: in Lamentations 1:17, the "enemies from around" are all those who dwell near Jerusalem and come to attack it.
4. It finally expresses the idea of being surrounded, encircled, or threatened from all sides — a total encirclement that makes escape impossible.
H5439J.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of turning or going around. The word appears in different forms in the Bible: sometimes as a noun (the surroundings), sometimes as an adverb (around), sometimes as a preposition (among, in the midst of). It is a very common word in Hebrew, playing on the natural image of circular movement: what turns around returns to its starting point.
H5439J.emploi: This word appears three times in the provided passages. In Lamentations 1:17, it describes the enemies coming from around to attack Jerusalem — it is a context of siege and threat. In Ezekiel 28:24 and 28:26, it speaks of the peoples who surround Israel and despise it: the word emphasizes the hostility of neighbors. In all these cases, it is less about simple geographical proximity than about pressure, encirclement, and hostility coming from all sides. The context is always one of danger or trial.
H5439J.portee: This word helps to understand how Israel found itself vulnerable, surrounded by enemies threatening it from all sides. For the Christian, it reminds that trials often come from everywhere at once, like an encirclement. But the promise of the text — that God will deliver His people and that the nations will know that He is God — shows that even total encirclement cannot prevent God from acting.

sens: Interwoven, densely woven and entangled together
That wraps or intertwines to form a compact and difficult-to-unravel whole
Figuratively: confused, intertwined, inextricably linked
H5440.detail:
1. The word concretely describes things that intertwine or weave together: it is the image of a net, of roots that wrap around each other. In Job 8:17, the roots of the plant are intertwined among the stones of the ground, forming a dense network.
2. It can also qualify a state where things are so mixed that they can no longer be easily separated. In Nahum 1:10, the enemy warriors are intertwined like thorns that cling to each other, so entangled that they cannot be untangled.
3. Figuratively, the word evokes the idea of confusion or interweaving: what is intertwined is complicated, difficult to analyze or separate.
H5440.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that evokes the action of braiding or intertwining fibers, threads. The basic image is that of weaving or plaiting. The word belongs to a small family of terms related to weaving and intertwining in the Old Testament. This root emphasizes the idea of a repeated and interwoven action rather than a simple juxtaposition.
H5440.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 8:17, it describes the roots of a plant that intertwine among the stones of a wall, highlighting the strength and tenacity of the vegetation. In Nahum 1:10, it qualifies the enemies intertwined like thorns, suggesting confusion and disorganization that make them vulnerable to divine judgment. In both cases, the word emphasizes a physical and concrete intertwining that makes the elements inseparable.
H5440.portee: This word reminds us that everything is interconnected: the forces of life and growth (the roots that intertwine to find their strength) and the forces of destruction (the enemies entangled and confused). For the believer, it illustrates how God can transform the entanglement of disorder into an instrument of judgment, and how true life is deeply rooted, even amid the toughest obstacles.

sens: A place covered with dense and tangled vegetation
A den or hiding place for an animal
A location from which a threat emerges
H5441.detail:
1. A thicket is an area covered with shrubs, bushes, and small trees intertwined with one another, where it is difficult to see clearly and move freely. It is dense and inextricable vegetation (Jeremiah 4:7).
2. The thicket naturally becomes a shelter, a place where wild animals hide or stay. In Jeremiah 4:7, the lion "leaps from his thicket": it is his den, the place from which he springs to attack.
3. By extension, the word can refer to a place from which a threat or danger emerges. The lion's thicket is not only an animal habitat but also the lair from which a destructive attack against the land originates.
H5441.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of intertwining or tangling. It refers to the concrete image of branches and stems that intertwine and form an impenetrable mass of vegetation. It is a rather specialized word in the Bible, which speaks of the natural world with its concrete and observable elements.
H5441.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 4:7. The context is that of a warning prophecy: the prophet describes an enemy (symbolized by a lion) that emerges from his thicket to ravage the land. The image of the lion escaping from his densely wooded lair illustrates a formidable threat that arises from darkness. The thicket here is not a mere description of landscape, but an element of a poetic image of aggression and devastation.
H5441.portee: This image of the lion coming out of the thicket reminds us that danger can arise from hidden and dark places, and that only God knows what is being prepared in the shadows. For the people of Jeremiah, it was a warning to take seriously: the threats we do not see coming can be real and serious. The lion's thicket invites us to vigilance and trust in God rather than false security.

sens: A dense and inextricable mass of branches, thorns, and underbrush
The thick and impenetrable part of a forest
A tangle that holds or conceals something
H5442.detail:
1. The word primarily designates wild and dense vegetation, made up of intertwined brambles and thorns. In Genesis 22:13, Abraham discovers a ram caught in a bush by its horns: the animal is trapped, a prisoner of this tight network of vegetation.
2. It also describes the dense part of a forest, the area that cannot be easily traversed. In Isaiah 10:34, the text speaks of the thickets of the forest that the Mighty One overturns with the axe: these are the thick and compact areas of the woods.
3. The image can also represent what burns and destroys: in Isaiah 9:17, wickedness "burns the thickness of the forest," like a fire that devours the brambles and thorns. The bush thus becomes a symbol of what burns and collapses.
H5442.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that likely means "intertwined" or "knotted together." The basic image is that of a tangle: branches and thorns that intertwine and knot together, making passage impossible. This compactness and density are at the heart of the meaning of the word.
H5442.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always to evoke wild and thick vegetation. In Genesis 22:13, it refers to a real bush where an animal is caught. In Psalms 74:5 and Isaiah 9:17, 10:34, the word describes rather a compact, impassable forest area, which serves as a backdrop for images of destruction (fire, axe). The context thus oscillates between the concrete bush and the thick forest, but always with the idea of a dense and difficult-to-cross tangle.
H5442.portee: This word reminds us that God provides for our needs in often unexpected ways: the ram hidden in the bush becomes the substitute sacrifice at the very moment Abraham needs it. It also invites the reader to see in the wild and thick nature an image of what resists, what burns, what collapses under divine judgment. It is a concrete word that anchors faith in the reality of the created world.

sens: Stringed musical instrument, triangular in shape, composed of four strings
Instrument used in royal orchestras and official ceremonies of the ancient world
H5443.detail:
1. The psaltery is a stringed musical instrument, triangular in shape, equipped with four strings. It is similar to the lyre, capable of producing melodious sounds. In Daniel 3, it is mentioned among the instruments of a great royal orchestra intended to accompany a religious ceremony imposed by the king.
2. The psaltery was a prestigious instrument, reserved for great official occasions. Its use in the decree of King Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 3:5) places it alongside other noble instruments like the trumpet and the guitar, signaling a manifestation of the royal and religious power of the Babylonian monarch.
H5443.origine: The Hebrew word שַׂבְּכָא comes from a root that evokes the triangular or woven shape of the instrument. It is a word borrowed from the vocabulary of the peoples of Western Asia, reflecting the cultural exchange between Mesopotamia and Israel during the Exile. The analogous Greek word ψαλτήριον (psaltery) has the same origin and meaning.
H5443.emploi: This word appears only four times in the Bible, all in chapter 3 of Daniel, in verses 5, 7, 10, and 15. It appears in the context of the decree of King Nebuchadnezzar ordering all peoples to bow down before the golden statue he has erected, at the sound of an orchestra including the psaltery. The word recurs in each enumeration of the musical instruments in this account of civil disobedience, emphasizing the magnitude and solemnity of the imposed ceremony.
H5443.portee: The psaltery reminds us that earthly power — even that of a great king — seeks to be worshiped through spectacle and sensory seduction. What stands out in the account of Daniel is that three young men refuse to bow down, even in the face of this impressive musical and political display. For the Christian reader, this word invites discernment between the beauty of creation (music, art) and idolatry, between enjoying the goods of the world and being seduced by what distances us from God.

sens: Warrior of David who fought the Philistine giants
Military chief of the eighth month in the royal army
Man from the tribe of Judah, from the family of the Zerahites
H5444.detail: Sibbecai is a renowned warrior in the service of King David. He belongs to the elite of the royal army and stands out for his victories against the enemies of Judah. In 2 Samuel 21:18, he kills Saph, one of the Philistine giants of the race of Rapha, during a battle at Gob. His courage in battle earns him a place among David's "Thirty," meaning the king's elite warriors (1 Chronicles 11:29). Beyond his role in combat, Sibbecai holds an important administrative position: he is appointed commander of the eighth division of the army, responsible for twenty-four thousand men for the eighth month of the year (1 Chronicles 27:11). He is from Hushah and belongs to the genealogical family of the Zerahites, descendants of Zerah, one of the sons of Judah.
H5444.origine: The name Sibbecai means "weaver" or "one who weaves," formed from a Hebrew root evoking the action of weaving. This name likely describes the profession or manual skill of his ancestors, before the warrior who bears it distinguished himself in the battles of King David.
H5444.emploi: Sibbecai appears four times in the Bible, all occurrences taking place during the time of the united monarchy under David. He is first mentioned in 2 Samuel 21:18 for his victory over the giant Saph. The book of Chronicles, which records the history of the kingdom of Judah from a genealogical and administrative perspective, cites him three times: in the list of the "Thirty" elite warriors (1 Chronicles 11:29), in a second account of victory over a giant (1 Chronicles 20:4), and in the list of captains of the twelve divisions of the royal army (1 Chronicles 27:11). These texts present him as a trusted man of the king, both a valiant warrior and a high-ranking military officer.
H5444.portee: The figure of Sibbecai reminds the believer that God uses faithful and courageous men to protect His people against their enemies. His victory over the Philistine giants encourages us to see that, with faith and courage, even the most formidable adversaries can be defeated. His rise to administrative responsibilities shows that integrity and dedication lead to honorable positions.

sens: To carry a weight on oneself, to bear a burden
To endure a burden, a pain, a suffering
To carry on one's shoulders or back
To be charged with something, to have responsibility for it
H5445.detail:
1. To carry a weight on oneself literally means to bear a physical load: in Isaiah 46:7, one "carries" an idol and "loads it on the shoulder." It is the image of a burden transported from one place to another.
2. To endure a burden in a moral or spiritual sense means to bear a pain, a suffering, or an iniquity that weighs on someone: in Isaiah 53:4, the suffering servant "has borne" our pains, meaning he took them upon himself. In Lamentations 5:7, the ancestors committed sins and "we bear" their iniquity.
3. To carry on the shoulder or back refers to the specific physical action: Genesis 49:15 describes one who "bends his shoulder under the burden," accepting to take on a debt or obligation.
4. To be charged with something means to have responsibility or a burden: God says in Isaiah 46:4, "I will sustain you" until old age, meaning He will bear the weight of sustaining and keeping you.
H5445.origine: The Hebrew verb סָבַל comes from a root that evokes the idea of loading, of bearing a weight. Its basic image is that of a bearer who bends his back under a burden. This word belongs to the family of verbs related to transport and load. The noun סֵבֶל (tribute, corvée) comes from the same root and shows how the word has extended to everything one must bear: first a physical object, then a debt, and finally a moral suffering.
H5445.emploi: This verb appears eight times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in contexts of burden, responsibility, and suffering. In Genesis 49:15, it describes servitude to a tribute. In Isaiah 46:4, 7, it contrasts God who truly bears His people with the idols that are carried in vain. It is in Isaiah 53:4 and 53:11 that the word takes on its deepest meaning: the suffering servant "bears" the sufferings and iniquities of the people — not literally on his shoulders, but by taking them upon himself, by assuming them. This spiritual meaning — to bear a moral or spiritual burden — thus becomes central in the theology of substitution and redemption.
H5445.portee: This word reveals how the Bible understands suffering and salvation: to bear a burden is not just to passively endure it, but to assume it, to take it on. When Isaiah 53:4 says that the Messiah "has borne" our pains, the text declares that He voluntarily took them upon Himself — not by force, but by love. This illuminates the meaning of the cross: Jesus bore our sins and our sufferings, He bore the weight in our place.

sens: That can bear a weight, support a load without bending
That has the necessary solidity to last and fulfill its function
H5446.detail:
1. The original Hebrew word first evokes the idea of carrying or supporting: it is a stone, a foundation, a structure capable of bearing the weight placed upon it. In Ezra 6:3, King Cyrus orders that the rebuilt temple have "solid" foundations — meaning capable of bearing the enormous weight of the sacred edifice without collapsing.
2. The idea expands: solid also means "robust," "durable," "reliable." The solid foundations of a building symbolize its stability and ability to endure over time. It is a word that refers to constructive quality: what is solid holds firm.
H5446.origine: The Hebrew verb סְבַל comes from a root that means "to bear" or "to support a load." It expresses the effort of the bearer or of one who supports a weight. By moving from the verb to the participle (the form used here), the word describes the quality of what is capable of bearing: something solid, stable, able to support.
H5446.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 6:3. The context is specific: the Persian king Cyrus authorizes the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem after the exile, and the order is that the temple be rebuilt with solid foundations. It is a technical construction term, applied to the foundations of the sanctuary. The unique usage underscores the importance of detail: a temple that glorifies God must be built with solidity, on durable foundations.
H5446.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that the work of God requires solidity. Even in a task as noble as the reconstruction of the temple, practical requirements cannot be overlooked: a house of God must be built on solid ground. It is an invitation not to neglect the foundations — spiritual or material — in what we undertake for the Lord.

sens: Physical load carried or transported
Forced labor, task
Weight of oppression or suffering
H5447.detail:
1. The burden is primarily a concrete load that one carries: construction materials, provisions, anything that weighs on a man's shoulders at work. In Nehemiah 4:17, during the reconstruction of the wall, some "carried or loaded burdens" with one hand while holding a weapon in the other — an image of intensive and dangerous labor.
2. The word also refers to imposed work, a task: it is the load required by the one in command. Jeroboam was placed in charge "of all the forced labor of the house of Joseph" (1 Kings 11:28) — an obligatory, generally arduous task.
3. Figuratively, it represents the weight of suffering or distress. Psalm 81:7 imagines God who "relieves the shoulder of the burden": it is the deliverance from servitude and oppression, the moment when pain ceases and the yoke becomes light.
H5447.origine: The Hebrew word סֵבֶל (sevel) comes from a root meaning "to carry" or "to load." It is related to the verb "sabel" (to suffer). The basic image is that of a body bending under a weight: a man loaded with burdens, bent over, tired. This word expresses both material and moral weight — the burden is what crushes, whether physical or spiritual.
H5447.emploi: The word sevel appears 3 times in the Hebrew Bible. It first describes the forced labor of Israel under kings (1 Kings 11:28) — a political and social context. It is then used for heavy materials to be transported during public works (Nehemiah 4:17). Finally, Psalm 81:7 gives it a theological significance: it is the burden of slavery in Egypt from which God delivers His people. The word is always on the side of the one who suffers, the one who is loaded or oppressed — never of the one who loads.
H5447.portee: The burden calls us to meditate on the load that others carry: those who work, those who serve against their will, those who are exploited. For the Christian, this word also says that God does not indefinitely leave His children bent under the weight. Psalm 81 promises that God "relieves" — He lightens, He liberates, He restores the one who cries out. It is a word of comfort for all who are overwhelmed.

sens: what weighs on someone, what one carries with effort
oppressive load imposed by a conqueror or oppressor
spiritual or moral weight that burdens
H5448.detail:
1. The burden is primarily what one carries, a physical load: this is the primary meaning of the word, as when one transports a heavy load that weighs on the shoulders. In Isaiah 9:3, "the yoke that weighed on him" evokes the material weight of the yoke carried by an oppressed man.
2. The word often refers to a load imposed by force — that of the conqueror or tyrant. In Isaiah 10:27, the prophet announces that the burden of the Assyrian, that is, the yoke of Assyrian oppression, will be removed from the people's shoulder. It is domination, the weight of political slavery.
3. By extension, the burden becomes what morally or spiritually overwhelms — the weight of judgment, guilt, or any form of imposed suffering. The prophetic context shows that it is a weight from which only God can deliver.
H5448.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of carrying, bearing a weight. It is related to other words that denote things that are carried or borne. The biblical burden is never neutral: it is almost always a painful weight, imposed or difficult to bear.
H5448.emploi: The word appears three times in the text of Isaiah, always in a prophetic context. In Isaiah 9:3, it characterizes the yoke of oppression. In Isaiah 10:27 and 14:25, it appears in the promise of deliverance: the burden will be removed, the yoke broken. Each usage emphasizes that this burden is intolerable and that only God's intervention can make it disappear. The image of the weight carried on the shoulders makes concrete the political and spiritual oppression.
H5448.portee: The word burden speaks to the heart of the one suffering under oppression: it names their weight, their pain. The biblical promise is not to accustom the believer to the burden, but to deliver them from it. Jesus will take up this image by promising that His yoke is easy and His burden is light, inviting to find true relief in Him.

sens: Heavy load carried on the back or in arms
Laborious and continuous physical work
Figuratively: weight, overwhelm
H5449.detail:
1. The burden is primarily a material, heavy, and concrete load that must be transported: in the great construction works of Solomon's temple, thousands of men had the job of "carrying burdens," meaning moving materials, stones, provisions (1 Kings 5:15; 2 Chronicles 2:2).
2. The word then refers to the effort, the toil of such work: those who carry burdens are exhausted, their strength fails, especially when they also have to clear debris and build a wall (Nehemiah 4:10).
3. By extension, the burden can be figurative: any load that overwhelms, any weight that one drags — a responsibility, suffering, anxiety — becomes a burden of the heart.
H5449.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to carry" or "to bear." The same root appears in other Hebrew words related to load and transport. The image is that of the weight placed on the shoulders: something that crushes, tires, that requires strength to bear.
H5449.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in the accounts of major public works: the construction of the temple by Solomon (1 Kings 5:15; 2 Chronicles 2:2, 2:18) and the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 4:10). It designates the work of laborers who must transport heavy loads — stones, materials, debris. The context is always that of a collective, imposed task that requires intense physical strength and can exhaust those who perform it.
H5449.portee: This word helps the reader understand the cost of a great project, a work that God wants to build: there is a physical price, a rough labor, a real fatigue. It also reminds us that any load, any weight — whether material or moral — can overwhelm us, and that we need strength to bear them. It is an invitation to compassion for those who work hard.

sens: Imposed and exhausting work done under compulsion
Authoritative burden imposed
Mandatory service required from a subjugated population
H5450.detail:
1. The word denotes hard and tiring work, forcibly imposed on those who have no choice. In Egypt, Pharaoh imposes "hard labor" on the Israelites to build his cities (Exodus 1:11), a burden so crushing that Moses witnesses it and sees his brothers struck by the taskmasters (Exodus 2:11). It is work that wears down both body and soul.
2. The word also describes the overall burden, the weight imposed on a subjugated people. Pharaoh refuses to allow the people to "interrupt their work" (Exodus 5:5), as he sees this interruption as a threat to his domination. Hard labor is the instrument of oppression.
3. By extension, it represents slavery itself: God promises to free the Israelites "from the burdens that the Egyptians impose on you" (Exodus 6:6-6:7), where "hard labor" summarizes all servitude, the absence of freedom, and systematic exploitation.
H5450.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to bear" or "to carry a burden." Sibla literally designates what one carries, what weighs on someone — initially a heavy object, then by extension anything that constitutes a crushing burden, physical or social. The family of words derived from it always speaks of a weight, an obligation that crushes.
H5450.emploi: This word appears 6 times in the Old Testament, exclusively in the account of Israel's oppression in Egypt (Exodus 1-6). It recurs like a refrain to describe the regime that Pharaoh imposes on the Hebrews: first established as a system of forced labor (Exodus 1:11), it becomes the emblem of Egyptian tyranny, the cry of the oppressed people. Moses himself sees it and is moved (Exodus 2:11). Pharaoh imposes it firmly (Exodus 5:4-5:5). And God promises to save His people by delivering them from this yoke specifically (Exodus 6:6-6:7). The word encapsulates the entire reality of slavery: daily, institutionalized, inhumane violence.
H5450.portee: This word reminds the reader that oppression is real, that the suffering of forced labor is not a detail but the very heart of slavery. It also shows that God sees this suffering, that He is moved by it, and that He acts to put an end to it. For the Christian, it is an encouragement: the burdens we carry, God knows them and wants to free us from them.

sens: Cluster of grains at the top of a cereal stalk
Word pronounced as a sign of recognition between tribes
Distinction or mark of identity
H5451.detail:
1. An ear of grain is the upper part of a cereal plant, formed of small grains tightly packed together at the end of the stalk. It is the whole that is harvested and threshed to yield the crop. In Judges 12:6, this word becomes the test allowing the Gileadites to recognize the Ephraimites: the latter pronounced "sibboleth" with a different sound, thus revealing their origin.
2. The word is used as a signal of identification: pronouncing "shibboleth" or "sibboleth" correctly shows to which tribe one belongs. This pronunciation distinguishes enemies from allies in times of war, a trivial detail of language becoming a matter of life or death.
3. Figuratively, it represents any distinctive mark that reveals a person's true identity, which they cannot hide.
H5451.origine: The Hebrew word shibboleth literally means "ear" or "stream" according to some theories. Its initial image is that of a grain plant in summer, recognizable by its characteristic shape. The confusion between sounds reflects the dialectical differences among the tribes of Israel: the Ephraimites had a distinctive accent or pronunciation that betrayed them, just as the shape of an ear identifies the type of grain.
H5451.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 12:6, during the battle between Gilead and Ephraim. After the defeat of the Ephraimites, the Gileadites control the fords of the Jordan and ask each fugitive to pronounce the word "shibboleth." Those who say "sibboleth" are identified as Ephraimites and are immediately executed. The context is one of brutal tribal vengeance, where the simple pronunciation of a word becomes an instrument of massacre: forty-two thousand Ephraimites perish because of this language difference.
H5451.portee: This passage teaches how tiny details — a pronunciation — can reveal who we truly are and where we come from. For the believer, it serves as a reminder that one cannot hide their true identity for long: our words and accents betray our hearts. It is also a warning against tribal or partisan intolerance that leads to killing in the name of minor differences.

sens: To have the intention or plan to do something
To think that something can or should happen
To seek to accomplish, to propose to
H5452.detail: 1. The verb first expresses a firm intention, a project one proposes to accomplish: in Daniel 7:25, the beast will speak words against God and "hope" to change the times and the law, meaning it will intend to modify them, it will attempt to do so. 2. In the background, there is also the idea of waiting or counting on something: the intention rests on a certain confidence that the act will take place or succeed. 3. It is less a passive waiting than an active waiting, tinged with will: one hopes by acting, by attempting.
H5452.origine: This Aramaic word (the language spoken by the Jews during the exile and post-exilic period) is close to the Hebrew "shabar" (שָׂבַר), which means "to wait" or "to hope." Both evoke the idea of a future-oriented expectation, that of one who counts on something or proposes to bring it about.
H5452.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 7:25, in Daniel's vision of future kingdoms. The beast (the last empire) "hopes" to change the times and the law of God — that is, it has the audacity to form the foolish project of modifying the order established by the Most High. This context shows a mad and impious hope, that of a creature that imagines it can thwart God's decrees. The word highlights the pride of this adversary: not only does it act, but it does so with the presumptuous intention of succeeding.
H5452.portee: For the believer, this verse reminds us that nothing and no one, no matter how powerful, can truly hope to change God's plans or His law. Even empires that seem invincible can only "imagine" they can oppose it. It is a source of confidence: while the enemy places its hope in impossible projects, the saint can entrust their hopes to the one whose purpose cannot be altered.

sens: City located between the borders of Damascus and Hamath
H5453.detail: Sibraim is a city mentioned in the prophetic vision of Ezekiel regarding the new borders of the territory of Israel. It is located between the border of Damascus and that of Hamath, two major regions of antiquity. This name appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 47:16, where the prophet enumerates the cities and landmarks that mark the northern limits of the restored land.
H5453.origine: The name Sibraim literally means "double hope" in Hebrew, composed of sib (hope) and the double "a-yim." It is a geographical name that designated a real locality from biblical times, in the northern Levant region, although it is not otherwise attested in current historical sources. Its location between Damascus and Hamath suggests a city of strategic importance in the ancient Near Eastern geography.
H5453.emploi: Sibraim is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 47:16. It appears in the context of the prophetic vision where Ezekiel describes the new borders of the territory of Israel to come. The prophet lists a series of cities and places that will serve as territorial markers: Sibraim figures as an important landmark marking the transition between the borders of Damascus and Hamath, two key areas of ancient Levantine geography.

sens: son of Cush, ancestor of the Cushites
H5454.detail: Sabta is the name of a man from the time of the Patriarchs, son of Cush and brother of Seba, Havilah, Raamah, Sabtechah, and Nimrod. He appears in the genealogy of peoples in chapter 10 of Genesis and is mentioned again in the genealogical lists of the first epistle to the Corinthians. His name means "striking" or "one who strikes," an image of strength or power.
H5454.origine: The name Sabta, whose variant is Sabtechah, literally means "striking." It designates a distant ancestor in the lineage of Noah, through his son Cush, who is himself the father of the Cushite peoples (peoples of the southeast: Arabia, Ethiopia, regions of the Persian Gulf). The name likely reflects traits or qualities associated with the founder of this group.
H5454.emploi: Sabta is mentioned only twice in the Bible, both times in genealogical lists: in Genesis 10:7, where he is listed among the sons of Cush, and in 1 Chronicles 1:9, which repeats the same genealogy. There is no account or event related to Sabta himself: his name appears only to mark genealogical continuity and identify the ancestors of the ancient peoples known to the Hebrews.

sens: Son of Cush, ancestor of the peoples of East Africa
H5455.detail: Sabteca is one of the five sons of Cush listed in the biblical genealogies. He represents an ancient people or lineage associated with the descendants of Noah through Ham. His name appears in the genealogical lists of Genesis and Chronicles without a specific account, simply to establish the lineage of ancient peoples.
H5455.origine: The name Sabteca literally means "one who strikes" or "striker," formed from a Semitic root evoking the action of striking or conquering. He designates one of the five sons of Cush (H3568), whose name itself means "Ethiopia" or the black peoples of ancient Africa. This genealogical context places Sabteca among the peoples descended from Ham, son of Noah.
H5455.emploi: Sabteca appears only twice in the Bible, both times in parallel genealogical enumerations. He is mentioned in Genesis 10:7 among the five sons of Cush with Saba, Havilah, Sabta, Raamah, and Nimrod. The same list reappears in 1 Chronicles 1:9, confirming Sabteca's rank in the order of Ham's descendants. These biblical genealogical lists aimed to establish the relationships between pre-flood and post-flood peoples, without providing details about the life or history of Sabteca himself.

sens: To bow deeply, in a posture of absolute humility
To pay homage through this gesture
To worship by prostrating oneself before a deity or an idol
H5456.detail:
1. To prostrate oneself is primarily to bow the body to the ground, face to the ground or at least very low, to express total submission. It is the very gesture of one who recognizes their nothingness before another. In Isaiah 44:19, a man speaks of prostrating himself "before a piece of wood," showing the ridiculousness of this gesture applied to a worthless idol.
2. This gesture becomes an act of recognition or homage towards the one before whom one prostrates. It is to acknowledge the authority, greatness, or power of that person through a body language that does not deceive.
3. To prostrate oneself takes on a religious meaning when performed before a deity or an idol. In Isaiah 44:17, a man "prostrates himself before it [the idol], he worships it," uniting the physical gesture with the act of religious worship. The word then describes the entirety of the worship rendered to false gods.
H5456.origine: The verb sagad comes from a root that evokes the idea of falling or bowing down. In Aramaic, the cognate segid (סְגִד) means "to pay homage" or "to make homage," which shows that this verb carries the idea of submission expressed by the body. It is a concrete word that paints the physical image before evoking the spiritual attitude.
H5456.emploi: The verb appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, all in the discourse of the prophet Isaiah against idolatry. In Isaiah 44:15, 44:17, and 44:19, Isaiah mocks the absurdity of the idolater who takes wood, burns half of it to warm himself and bake his bread, then makes a god with the rest and prostrates himself before it—highlighting the moral and rational folly of idolatry. In Isaiah 46:6, the word again designates the gesture of idolatrous worship. The constant context is that of a physical gesture of worship rendered to idols, always presented as the expression of religious deception.
H5456.portee: This word teaches that true worship must be directed to the living God alone, and not to human creations. The spectacle of a man prostrating himself before a piece of wood he has made himself challenges the reader: to what or whom do you really pay homage with your life? Prostration is the gesture that engages the whole being, body and soul, and that is why it should only be offered to the true God.

sens: to bow down to the ground in a sign of deep respect
to acknowledge the supremacy of someone or something through a posture of submission
to offer worship to a deity or an idol
H5457.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to prostrate oneself is to throw oneself to the ground, face to the ground, before a person of high rank. It is the gesture of a vassal before a king or a subject before their master. Daniel 2:46 shows this: Nebuchadnezzar "fell on his face and prostrated himself before Daniel."
2. This gesture expresses the recognition of absolute authority, of a power that dominates. It is to say with the body: "You are above me, I submit myself." In Daniel 3:5-7, when the king's music sounds, all the peoples "prostrated themselves and worshiped the golden statue."
3. When this gesture is directed towards a deity or an idol, it takes on the meaning of religious worship, of adoration. The refusal to prostrate oneself before the golden idol (Daniel 3:11-12) was for the three young men a refusal to acknowledge any religious authority other than that of the God of Israel.
H5457.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of bowing down, of bending the body. In the Aramaic of the Old Testament, "segid" retains this sense of physical lowering, of a gesture of humiliation or reverence. The context of the Book of Daniel, written in Aramaic, shows this word used to describe the practices of Persian court and the religious rituals of the Babylonian world.
H5457.emploi: This verb appears 11 times in the Book of Daniel, all occurrences being in Daniel 2-3, the context of the statues and the challenges imposed by Nebuchadnezzar. The meaning does not vary: it is always about prostrating oneself before an authority (the king or his idol). In Daniel 2:46, it is the king who pays homage to Daniel by recognizing him as wise. Then in Daniel 3, it is the royal order that imposes on all peoples to worship the golden statue; the refusal of the three young men (Daniel 3:12, 3:18) shows that worshiping an idol is a religious act that engages the believer's conscience.
H5457.portee: For the Christian reader, this word illustrates the conflict between loyalty to earthly powers and faithfulness to God alone. The three young men refuse to prostrate themselves before the idol, even if it costs them their apparent lives. The word "worship" reminds us that some acts of submission are never neutral: to prostrate oneself is to recognize a spiritual authority. True worship belongs to God alone.

sens: What encloses, what covers
What protects or encloses the heart
H5458.detail:
1. The word literally designates what encloses or wraps something, like a protective layer or container. In Job 28:15, it refers to fine gold, precious, wrapped or enclosed — the image is that of a precious material protected or hidden in its natural casing.
2. Figuratively, in Hosea 13:8, the "envelope" of the heart represents the protection that the heart has given itself, the emotional or moral defenses that humans erect. God threatens to tear this protective envelope: it is as if the heart has closed in on itself, and God will force this barrier, penetrate this inner fortress to judge what is hidden there.
H5458.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes enclosure and covering. It is related to verbal forms meaning "to enclose" or "to surround." The basic image is that of something covered, locked away, protected by an outer layer — hence its use for fine gold, a precious metal often buried or wrapped in its ore.
H5458.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 28:15, in the long discourse on wisdom and riches, it qualifies fine gold as a precious material that cannot be bought, wrapped or enclosed in its very nature. In Hosea 13:8, the prophet uses it figuratively and dramatically: God, like a furious lioness, will tear the envelope of the hardened heart of the people. The meaning thus shifts from the concrete (material envelope) to the spiritual (the shell of the heart closed to God).
H5458.portee: This word invites the reader to see that the heart can close, protect itself, harden — to give itself an impermeable envelope to God. But it also reminds that this protection is fragile in the face of divine justice and power. For the believer, it is a call not to let one's heart become encased in sin and rebellion, for God has the ability and intention to break down any barrier.

sens: Property, object, or wealth that one possesses personally
What has great value in the eyes of the possessor
People or person that God reserves as His precious possession
H5459.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a possession, a good that one holds personally: it is what one "has" and can affirm is ours. David says that he "possesses" gold and silver for the house of God (1 Chronicles 29:3).
2. But this is not just any good: it is a valuable possession, a treasure that one particularly cherishes. The word evokes something precious, chosen, that one sets aside for oneself.
3. The Bible applies it especially to the relationship between God and Israel: God says that the Israelites "will be My treasured possession among all peoples" (Exodus 19:5), not as slaves, but as an elected people, a possession dear to His heart. Israel is the personal treasure of the Lord.
H5459.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of setting apart, reserving for oneself. It is related to the idea of "separation" or "exclusive choice." In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it is often rendered by a Greek word meaning also "particular property." This notion of a precious good, chosen and kept for oneself, is at the heart of the term.
H5459.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the Pentateuch and the Psalms. It is used significantly to describe the relationship of the Lord with Israel: "you will be a people that belongs to Him" (Deuteronomy 7:6; 14:2; 26:18; Psalms 135:4). It is the election of Israel that is at stake. It is also found in the common sense of "possession" or "wealth" (1 Chronicles 29:3), and in eschatological contexts (Malachi 3:17). The theological meaning dominates: to be a possession of God is to be loved and kept.
H5459.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the believer that he is chosen, precious, cherished by God. There is no cold relationship between God and His people: God calls us His personal treasure. For a Christian, this means that our value does not depend on what we possess or accomplish, but on the fact that God has chosen us and keeps us as His most cherished possession.

sens: High-ranking officer in the administration of an empire
Responsible for a province or royal domain
Chief placed above other magistrates
Advisor to the king invested with authority
H5460.detail: 1. In the Babylonian empire and the Persian court, the steward is a high official appointed by the king to govern a province or oversee an important sector of administration. After interpreting the dreams of King Nebuchadnezzar, Daniel receives this title: "he made him chief over all the wise men of Babylon" (Daniel 2:48), which shows that the steward combines administrative responsibilities and authority over the kingdom's experts. 2. The steward ranks among the highest officials of the state, alongside satraps (governors of large regions) and magistrates. During the consecration of the golden statue, "King Nebuchadnezzar summoned the satraps, the stewards, and the governors" (Daniel 3:2), establishing a hierarchy where the steward occupies a prestigious position. 3. It is a position of trust, reserved for those who enjoy royal favor and whose intelligence and loyalty are esteemed. The word emphasizes less a technical function than a direct authority: one who commands, who orders, and whose word is law in his domain.
H5460.origine: Aramaic word formed from a root meaning "to place" or "to establish" (the Hebrew root שׂגג or a variant related to the verb "to dominate"). The term designates one who is "established" in authority, that is, instituted as chief by the king. In the Segond, its Hebrew root sagan (סָגָן) has the same meaning: a man of power to whom governance is entrusted.
H5460.emploi: The word appears only five times in the Bible, all in the book of Daniel, and always in a Persian or Babylonian context: Daniel 2:48, 3:2-3, 3:27, and 6:7. It describes the power structures of foreign empires confronted with God. The varied usage shows that "steward" can designate a high official personally serving the king (like Daniel) or provincial magistrates who are part of the royal council. In Daniel 2:48, the word emphasizes the exceptional elevation of the young exile; in the following verses, it situates the steward within a state hierarchy. The context is always that of imposing human authority, against which God displays His power (deliverance from the furnace, victory of Daniel).
H5460.portee: This word reminds us that, even in the most powerful empires of this world, human authority remains subordinate to God. Daniel, promoted to steward, owes his wisdom and honor only to his faithfulness to God, and it is God who protects and establishes him. For the believer, it is a lesson: human power and prestige are but wind; only God's favor is stable and bears fruit.

sens: Officer or governor who exercises administrative authority for a sovereign
Military leader or high-ranking dignitary
Local official responsible for administering a region or city
H5461.detail:
1. The magistrate is an officer or governor who represents the authority of a king or empire. They are a subordinate of the central power, tasked with maintaining order and managing a province or region. In Nehemiah 5:7, Nehemiah complains to the magistrates about exploiting their brothers through usury, showing that they hold authority over the civil and economic affairs of their people.
2. In a military context, the magistrate is often a war chief or high-ranking general. Jeremiah 51:23 lists those whom God breaks: shepherds, plowmen, governors, and chiefs—a list that descends from the powerful to the simple household masters, placing magistrates among the great authorities destroyed.
3. They are also a local official or civil administrator with delegated jurisdiction. Upon returning from exile in Judea, the magistrates work alongside the nobles to organize the people (Nehemiah 7:5), illustrating their role as executors of public administration.
H5461.origine: The Hebrew word סָגָן comes from a root meaning "to be high" or "to elevate." It is a term borrowed from the administrative vocabulary of Mesopotamian empires, where the magistrate was a high official or prefect. The Aramaic סְגַן (H5460) is a very close variant, and these two forms appear side by side in texts from the Persian period, reflecting the political context in which Israel lived under foreign domination.
H5461.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the Old Testament, primarily in Nehemiah (8 occurrences)—where the magistrates are leaders of the people after the exile—and in the prophets Jeremiah and Ezekiel (7 occurrences). In Nehemiah, the magistrates are Israelite officials who must assist Nehemiah in his civil and religious restoration. In the prophecies against Babylon (Jeremiah 51) and Egypt (Ezekiel 23), the magistrate is a warrior or foreign dignitary, luxuriously dressed and equipped. The word also designates minor vassal kings or authorities under Assyrian domination (Isaiah 41:25). Everywhere, the magistrate occupies an intermediate rank: below the sovereign but above the common people.
H5461.portee: This word reminds us that all human authority—whether civil, military, or administrative—is subordinate to that of God and must give an account before Him. When magistrates abuse their power (as in Nehemiah 5), the prophetic conscience accuses them. Conversely, the faithful magistrate who carries out a just mission with integrity (like Nehemiah himself) becomes an instrument of God's purpose for His people. It is an invitation to see every responsibility as a stewardship for which one will be held accountable.

sens: Close an opening, a door, a passage
Imprison someone, confine them
Deliver someone into the hands of an enemy or a judge
Block, prevent from advancing, isolate
Pure gold, without alloy
H5462.detail:
1. To close an opening or a door: this is the physical action of closing, whether it be a door, a house, or a passage. After creating woman, God "closed up the flesh" from Adam's side (Genesis 2:21). During the flood, Noah enters the ark and "the Lord shut him in" (Genesis 7:16).
2. To imprison someone, confining them in a closed space: this means to confine a person, often for punishment or isolation. During leprosy, the sick were confined outside the camp (Leviticus 13 to 14). The prophet Ezekiel was "shut up" in his house to be limited in his movements (Ezekiel 3:24).
3. To deliver someone into the hands of an enemy or justice: this means to hand over a person, often against their will, to someone else. David tells Saul: "The Lord will deliver you into my hand" (1 Samuel 24:19). It also carries the idea of "closing someone to" something, meaning depriving them of something: the Lord "made barren" the rival of Samuel's mother, literally "closed her womb" (1 Samuel 1:5-6).
4. To block or prevent from advancing: this means to bar the way, isolating a besieged city. Jericho was "tightly shut" because of the fear of the Israelites (Joshua 6:1).
5. Pure gold, precious metal without alloy: this meaning derives from the idea of closure and completeness. All the cups and dishes of King Solomon were of "pure gold" (1 Kings 10:21), which evokes perfection and the absence of mixture.
H5462.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root denoting the action of closing or shutting. The primary meaning is very concrete: to close a door, a passage. The ideas of "imprisoning" and "delivering" naturally follow: to close someone in a place is to deliver them to that confinement, and to deliver someone to an enemy is to "close" them to their freedom. The meaning of "pure gold" is less obvious: it may stem from the idea of a material "closed" upon itself, without flaw or mixture, symbolizing completeness.
H5462.emploi: This verb appears 87 times in the Old Testament, primarily in historical and poetic narratives. Concrete usages dominate: doors and houses that close (Genesis 2:21, Leviticus 14:38, Joshua 2:5), people confined or imprisoned (Leviticus 13-14 for lepers, Ezekiel 3:24 for the prophet). The meaning of "delivering" is frequent in contexts of war and justice: God "delivers" His enemies into the hands of David (1 Samuel 17:46) or Solomon. The meaning of "pure gold" appears several times in the description of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:20-21, 1 Kings 10:21). The notion of isolation or blockage appears in siege narratives (Joshua 6:1, Isaiah 24:10).
H5462.portee: This verb shows how God controls circumstances: He closes the doors of the ark during the flood, He delivers enemies into the hands of His servants. For the believer, "closing" reminds us that our doors, our lives, our hearts are under God's control. It is a word of comfort in adversity: even in prison or exile, one does not escape His providence. The image of pure gold also suggests purity and completeness in divine worship.

sens: Close, shut an opening or passage
Block, obstruct (a mouth, lips)
Keep closed, hold captive
H5463.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to close something in a way that blocks access or opening: to close a door, a mouth, a passage. It is the physical action of bringing the two sides of an opening together to make it inaccessible.
2. An important nuance is that of blocking or obstructing: to close someone's lips or mouth to prevent them from speaking. This is what happens in Daniel 6:22, where God shuts the mouths of the lions so that Daniel is not devoured—the angel of God neutralized their ferocity.
3. The usage can also express the idea of imprisoning or retaining: to keep something or someone in such a way that nothing can escape. It is a gentle captivity, a paradoxical protection.
H5463.origine: The word comes from a Semitic root that primitively means "to close" or "to silence." The Aramaic verb סְגַר (se.gar) is of the same family as the Hebrew סָגַר (sa.gar), which is very common in the Old Testament. The underlying image is that of closing a door or an orifice to block any passage.
H5463.emploi: This verb appears only once in our sources, in Daniel 6:22, in the Aramaic passive. It is the climactic moment of Daniel's story in the lion's den: after a terrifying night, the prophet reports to Darius that God sent His angel to shut the mouths of the lions. The use of the word shows a supernatural intervention: it is not simply that the lions were full or drowsy, but that God actively neutralized their aggressiveness. The word emphasizes the helplessness of creatures against the divine will and the absolute protection that God can grant to His faithful ones.
H5463.portee: This account reveals that God masters the impossible and protects those who fear Him. Closing the mouths of lions—beasts considered merciless—illustrates that no force on earth, no natural danger can escape the control of the living God. For the reader, it is an assurance: when one remains faithful in trial, God can radically transform seemingly deadly circumstances. The word also reminds us that divine protection is not a coincidence, but a voluntary act on His part.

sens: Continuous rain that falls regularly and without interruption
Tenacious rain that imposes itself and does not cease
H5464.detail:
1. This word refers to rain that stubbornly falls, drop by drop, without respite — not a violent deluge, but a steady flow that lasts. In Proverbs 27:15, the Bible compares it to a leaky gutter in a house: annoying, exhausting, impossible to ignore. It is the rain that slowly but surely soaks everything, infiltrating everywhere.
2. Figuratively, the same verse likens it to a quarrelsome woman — someone who continually returns to accusations and disputes, wearing down the listener by the very persistence of her grievances, rather than by their violence.
H5464.origine: This Hebrew noun comes from a root that expresses the idea of closure or uninterrupted continuity. The image is that of water flowing without interruption, drop by drop: a rain that encloses, envelops, and does not let you go. It is a rare word in the Old Testament, specialized to express not quantity or intensity, but tenacity.
H5464.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Proverbs 27:15. It is placed in a moral comparison: the persistent rain, just like the leaky gutter, is the perfect image of an endless quarrel. The wise man uses it to show how an irritable person, who continually returns to disputes, exhausts those who endure her — not through violent outbursts, but through daily and predictable weariness.
H5464.portee: This verse teaches that some relational ills do not come from spectacular crises, but from daily wear: a harsh word repeated, a constant reproach, a perpetually tense atmosphere. For a Christian, it is an invitation to examine how one speaks and quarrels — to recognize that the persistence of reproach or conflict causes more damage than intensity. It is a call to gentleness and restraint in relationships.

sens: Piece of wood or metal pierced with holes, intended to immobilize the feet of a prisoner
Shackles that symbolize captivity and oppression
Limitation imposed on freedom of movement
H5465.detail:
1. A yoke is a device made of wood or metal, pierced with holes, in which the feet of a prisoner or slave are confined to prevent escape or free movement. It is an instrument of chaining or confinement. Job mentions it when he says: "Why put my feet in the yoke" (Job 13:27).
2. The yoke symbolically represents captivity, servitude, and oppression — the state of one who is no longer free. When Job speaks of his feet being put "in the yoke," he describes his trial as a form of confinement, a loss of freedom in the face of suffering.
3. The yoke limits the steps of the one who bears it: it "watches all my movements" and sets "a limit to my steps" (Job 13:27 and 33:11). It expresses the idea of imposed constraint, a restriction of the freedom to act.
H5465.origine: The Hebrew word sad literally designates a piece of worked wood or metal — the idea of a carved or assembled piece. It is a concrete and technical term, with no major derivatives in the Bible. It simply translates the physical reality of these detention instruments, used in prisons and mines of the ancient world.
H5465.emploi: The word sad appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the book of Job. Job bitterly complains about it: in Job 13:27, he asks why God puts his feet in the yoke and watches all his movements, then in Job 33:11, Eliphaz takes up this image to speak of the yoke that God would have placed on his feet. In these two occurrences, the yoke is an image of trial, of the limit imposed on freedom, and of divine surveillance — which Job feels as oppression rather than protection.
H5465.portee: The yoke reminds us that suffering can give the impression of being shackled, immobilized, with no way out. But for the believer, it is an invitation to ask: am I really a prisoner, or am I called to seek the meaning of what limits me? Job's words urge us to express our distress before God rather than suppress it.

sens: Fine linen garment worn over others or alone at night
Rectangular piece of linen fabric used as outerwear
Valuable item exchanged in markets and contracts
H5466.detail:
1. The linen shirt is a garment made from fine cloth, intended to be worn directly or over other clothing. It is a precious and sought-after fabric, a sign of social status or wealth. In Samson's riddles, these linen shirts are offered as prizes for anyone who could discover the answer (Judges 14:12).
2. The word refers to the piece of fabric itself, worked and tailored into a rectangular garment. This type of shirt could serve as the sole garment during the night or be worn on important occasions, reflecting its quality and fineness.
3. These shirts are items of trade and exchange: the wise woman of Proverbs 31:24 makes and sells them, while Isaiah 3:23 lists them among the beautiful objects owned by the women of Jerusalem before divine judgment. They represent wealth, labor, and commerce.
H5466.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew סָדִין (sadir or sadin), probably related to roots expressing what extends or covers. Its use in the Bible shows that it is a textile of value, associated with prosperity and precious goods.
H5466.emploi: This word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always to designate this fine linen garment. In the story of Samson (Judges 14:12-13), the shirts are prestigious prizes offered to anyone who could solve his riddle. In Proverbs 31:24, they testify to the profitable work of a diligent woman who makes and sells them. Isaiah 3:23 lists them among the luxurious ornaments of the women of Jerusalem condemned. In all contexts, the linen shirt represents a valuable good, an object of trade, or a high prize.
H5466.portee: This word reminds us that wealth and material goods have a place in the daily life of the Old Testament, but also that their possession can become a source of pride or attachment. In Samson's case, the shirts symbolize a material stake; in the case of the woman in Proverbs, the honest work that produces these goods; in Isaiah, the vanity of luxurious adornment before judgment. It is a window into the economy, clothing, and values of biblical times.

sens: Canaanite city located near the Dead Sea
Symbol of perversion and grave sin
Example of God's justice against evil
H5467.detail:
1. Sodom is a Canaanite city that was located in the region of the Dead Sea and the Jordan, often mentioned alongside Gomorrah. It was one of the cities of Canaan and served as a geographical landmark (Genesis 10:19). Abraham observed this region and chose to distance himself from it, seeing the people of Sodom sinning grievously against the Lord (Genesis 13:10-13).
2. Sodom has become the biblical symbol of grave sin and moral perversion. The prophets compare the idolatrous people of Israel to Sodom to emphasize their distance from God: Isaiah declares that Israel boasts of its crime "like Sodom" (Isaiah 3:9), and Ezekiel reproaches Jerusalem for becoming worse than Sodom in its iniquity (Ezekiel 16:48-49).
3. Sodom illustrates God's judgment against evil: the Lord rained down fire and brimstone on the city (Genesis 19:24), making it a warning for future generations. The prophets invoke its destruction to demonstrate the certainty of divine punishment (Amos 4:11, Zephaniah 2:9).
H5467.origine: The name Sodom likely means "burning" or "the place that burns," which evokes its fate: annihilated by heavenly fire. The city was a historical and geographical reality during Abraham's time, but it has taken on a profound theological significance in the Bible, becoming the very type of divine judgment on human sin.
H5467.emploi: Sodom is mentioned 38 times in the Hebrew and Greek Bible, primarily in Genesis (the account of its destruction), but also in the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Amos, Zephaniah). Initially (Genesis 10, 13, 14), it is an ordinary Canaanite city; then it becomes the stage for divine judgment (Genesis 18-19). Subsequently, the prophets regularly mention it to threaten Israel or Judah with the same punishment, or to emphasize that God does not spare sin. Ezekiel uses it to instruct Jerusalem about its own culpabilities (Ezekiel 16:46-56).
H5467.portee: Sodom reminds the believer that persistent evil does not go unpunished, and that no human power can escape God's judgment. Its story also warns against moral pride and indifference to divine command. It is a call to repentance and the fear of God.

sens: State of disorder, unorganized mixture
Absence of clarity, logical arrangement
Spiritual and moral darkness
H5468.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes complete disorder, where things are out of place and order has vanished. In Job 10:22, "confusion" characterizes the abode of the dead: it is a place where shadow reigns without distinction, where everything mixes in darkness.

2. It also signifies the absence of clarity and structure: when everything is confused together, nothing is seen distinctly, nothing is understood. The deep darkness that Job speaks of is a confusion where light itself resembles darkness.

3. The word can also express a moral or spiritual situation of chaos, abandonment to dark powers — the image of the abode of the dead, a land without law or clarity.
H5468.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of arrangement or organization. When it is overturned or destroyed, it is confusion. It literally denotes what is scattered, mixed, without order. It is the opposite of God's ordered creation ("order" in Hebrew).
H5468.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 10:22. Job describes the abode of the dead — this underground region where shadows pile up — as a place of profound confusion. This is why the French translation chooses "confusion": the context emphasizes the total darkness, the absence of order, and the indistinct mixture of darkness that reigns there. The word belongs to the poetic and eschatological register.
H5468.portee: This verse reminds the believer that the world without God, and particularly the abode of the dead far from His presence, is characterized by chaos and spiritual darkness. It underscores the importance of walking in the light of God during our earthly life, and the hope that Christ brings in the face of this eternal confusion.

sens: round or cup-shaped form
vessel or container of rounded shape
female breast with rounded shapes
H5469.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a round and hollow shape, like that of a cup or bowl. In Song of Solomon 7:3, the breast is referred to as a "rounded cup": the image evokes a full and well-formed shape, capable of holding wine, a symbol of richness and sweetness.
2. By extension, it can refer to the container itself — a cup, a bowl — with the idea of curvature and elegance in its curves. It is the crafted object, shaped with grace.
3. Applied to the female body, it is a poetic image: the breast is compared to this delicate and rounded vessel. The allusion to "the wine that does not lack" reinforces the connection with abundance and sensuality.
H5469.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to turn" or "to be round." The same family produces other words related to circularity and spiral shape. The basic image is that of the potter's wheel: something that has been turned, shaped round. This type of word shows how Hebrew describes shapes by the movement that creates them.
H5469.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in the Song of Solomon in chapter 7. It is part of the loving discourse of the poem: the lover magnifies the beauty of his beloved by describing her with images of rounded and full shapes. This unique occurrence shows that the word was rare or literary, reserved for a poetic and laudatory register. The context is clearly one of celebrating feminine beauty.
H5469.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Bible speaks of the body and marital love without shame or reservation, using poetry and beauty. It is an invitation to recognize that creation — the feminine form, the senses — belongs to God's benevolent design. The Song affirms that mutual desire and admiration in marriage are holy and good.

sens: Building or place where prisoners are confined
Royal detention place, guarded and administered
State of deprivation of freedom
H5470.detail:
1. The word denotes a building intended to confine prisoners, often constructed in a round or circular shape for greater strength. In Genesis 39:20, Joseph is put in this prison where "the king's prisoners were confined": it is a physical place of confinement.
2. The prison is administered by a chief or director responsible for the inmates and security. In Genesis 39:21-22, the "chief of the prison" receives Joseph favorably and "placed under his supervision all the prisoners who were in the prison": it is an organized establishment with a hierarchy.
3. The word also denotes the state or condition of one who is held there: being in prison means being separated from the free world, deprived of liberty. In Genesis 40:3, the cupbearer and baker of the king are "confined in the prison," signifying their captivity.
H5470.origine: The Hebrew word סֹהַר (sohar) likely comes from a root evoking roundness or circularity (סוּר, "to turn"), as ancient prisons were often built in the shape of a tower or circular building. The word is exclusively used to designate the prison, notably the Egyptian royal prison in the story of Joseph.
H5470.emploi: The word appears six times, all in the account of Joseph in Egypt (Genesis 39–40). Joseph is thrown there after being falsely accused by Potiphar's wife. Despite his imprisonment, he finds favor with the chief of the prison, who entrusts him with great responsibilities (39:21-22). His fellow captives, the cupbearer and baker of Pharaoh, receive from him the interpretation of their dreams (40:5). The word describes both the physical place and the concrete experience of captivity that Joseph endures without losing faith.
H5470.portee: The story of Joseph in prison teaches that faithfulness to God remains possible even in injustice and confinement. Although wrongfully imprisoned, Joseph does not lose his trust in the Lord who "was with him" (39:23). This prison paradoxically becomes the place where his faith shines and where he gains the trust of others. For the Christian, this account shows that God can accomplish His purposes even when we go through situations of apparent defeat or oppression.

sens: Egyptian king or chief during the divided monarchy of Israel
H5471.detail: So is an Egyptian ruler mentioned only once in the Bible, at a time when the kingdom of Israel is divided and weakened. King Hoshea of Israel, who was to pay tribute to the powerful king of Assyria, sought help from So by sending messengers to Egypt (2 Kings 17:4). This action shows that So was powerful enough for the king of Israel to hope for his support against Assyria. However, So was unable to help him, and Hoshea was imprisoned by the king of Assyria.
