H5471.origine: The name So means "the hidden one" or "concealed" in Hebrew. It likely refers to an Egyptian ruler from the 8th century BC, perhaps the vizier or the chief of a region in Egypt rather than the reigning pharaoh. The exact historical identity remains debated among historians.
H5471.emploi: So appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 17:4. He is mentioned as king of Egypt at the time when the Assyrian king Sargon II besieges Samaria, the capital of the Northern Kingdom (Israel). Hoshea, the last king of Israel, had initially agreed to pay tribute to Assyria, then sought to revolt by allying with Egypt. This failed alliance hastened the fall of the kingdom of Israel around 722 BC.

sens: To move backward, to physically turn away
To beat a retreat, to be put to flight
To distance oneself from someone, to break a relationship
To abandon the right path, to turn away from God
To be unfaithful, to become a renegade
To be repelled, to fail in one's intentions
H5472.detail:
1. The verb first describes a physical movement: advancing then stopping and going back, like someone who retreats in the face of an obstacle or danger (Psalms 35:4: "Let those who seek my life retreat and be ashamed").
2. It then means to flee, to be chased, to retreat in a military sense: enemies are repelled in battle and must leave the field (Jeremiah 46:5: in this context, the armies retreat under defeat).
3. The word also expresses a relational break: distancing oneself from someone, ceasing to follow or trust them, like one steps away from a person (Psalms 78:57: Israel "turned away" from God and "was unfaithful").
4. Spiritually, it signifies apostasy: turning one's back on God, abandoning His covenant, ceasing to obey Him (Psalms 53:4: "All have gone astray" expresses this deviation from the moral and religious right path).
5. It can mean becoming unfaithful or a renegade, betraying one's promises, as in Zephaniah 1:6 where people "turn away" from the Lord and no longer seek Him.
6. Finally, the word expresses the idea of being repelled or rejected in one's efforts: to fail, to be thwarted, like a deceptive bow that deviates its arrow (Psalms 78:57).
H5472.origine: The Hebrew root sûg fundamentally means "to turn" or "to turn oneself." It evokes the movement of one who changes direction, pivots on oneself, or backs up. In Hebrew, this verb is closely related to the idea of diversion: first physical (to retreat, to go away), then moral and spiritual (to stray from good, from God). The same root appears in other forms to express various nuances of this movement of retreat or diversion.
H5472.emploi: The verb appears 14 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms (about ten occurrences) and in the prophetic books. In the supplication Psalms, it often describes the psalmist's enemies: they "retreat" confused (Psalms 35:4, 40:15, 70:3), defeated by God's intervention. In historical and prophetic contexts, it expresses Israel's unfaithfulness: the people "turn away" from the covenant (Psalms 78:57), "go astray" far from justice (Psalms 53:4). In Isaiah 50:5, the Servant of God asserts that he will not "retreat," that he will not turn away from his mission, which contrasts with the unfaithfulness of the people. The meaning thus oscillates between physical retreat (military or motor), the rejection of enemies, and the spiritual apostasy of the people.
H5472.portee: This verb reminds the believer of the seriousness of turning away from God: it is not only a defeat but also unfaithfulness, a deliberate choice to break the covenant. In contrast, the promise of the Psalms and Isaiah 50:5 invites the faithful not to retreat, to stand firm in the face of trials. Understanding this word helps to grasp why the Bible so fears apostasy: it is never a slight deviation, it is a complete turning away, an active refusal of God's presence and will.

sens: To form a barrier all around something or someone
To delimit a space by closing it on all sides
To protect or isolate by a fence
H5473.detail:
1. The literal meaning is to build a fence or barrier around an area: it is the idea of forming a physical limit, as one surrounds a field or garden with walls or hedges to protect or delimit it. In Song of Solomon 7:3, the body of the beloved is described as "a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies": the image evokes an enclosed, preserved, singular field.
2. Figuratively, to surround also means to circumscribe or enclose: it is to isolate something from its environment, making it distinct or inaccessible. The poetic use in the Song suggests a delicate separation, that of the beloved from the rest of the world.
H5473.origine: The Hebrew verb סוּג (sug) comes from a root that carries the idea of closing or enclosing. The word evokes the action of erecting a barrier or hedge around a space. Its unique occurrence in Song of Solomon 7:3 shows it applied to an image of beauty that is delimited and protected, giving both an aesthetic and protective nuance to the verb.
H5473.emploi: The verb סוּג appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 7:3. It is a poetic description of the body of the beloved: "a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies." This unique context shows that the word is used figuratively, to evoke not a literal enclosure, but the idea that the beloved is distinct, singular, isolated like a precious field surrounded by flowers. The rarity of the word makes it a term deliberately chosen by the poet for its rich imagery.
H5473.portee: This verb reminds the reader that beauty and value can be set apart and preserved. In the romantic language of the Song, to surround evokes protection and exclusivity: what is surrounded is unique and precious. For the believer, it also speaks of the distinction of one who belongs to God — preserved, set apart for a beautiful and holy purpose.

sens: Enclosed space intended to confine
Prison, place of captivity
Instrument of control and submission
H5474.detail:
1. A cage is a fenced or barred enclosure, generally intended to confine an animal. In Ezekiel 19:9, the lion, a symbol of the king of Israel, is placed in a cage with hooks in its nostrils, the concrete image of a wild animal made captive and controlled.

2. The word also figuratively designates a prison: a place of captivity where one is deprived of freedom. The context of the prophecy shows that this cage symbolizes the servitude of the king and his people before the king of Babylon.

3. By extension, the cage represents any instrument of control and subjugation: the means by which one renders someone harmless and submissive. The hooks in the nostrils of the lion reinforce this idea of complete domination and hostage of power.
H5474.origine: The Hebrew word sûgar comes from a root that evokes the idea of closure and confinement. It is related to the verb "to close" or "to shut." The starting image is that of a closed and secured space to keep something or someone inside, hence the meaning of cage or prison.
H5474.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 19:9. It is found in a prophecy against the leaders of Israel, compared to lion cubs: the prophet describes how the powerful and fierce lion is captured, chained (hooks in the nostrils) and confined in a cage, then dragged into captivity in Babylon. This unique occurrence concentrates all the force of the word: to show the humiliation and total loss of freedom of the once-majestic leader.
H5474.portee: This image of the cage teaches the reality of divine judgment on those who resist God and abuse power. It also shows that even the strongest, even the king, can be reduced to helplessness and servitude by the hand of God. For the believer, it reminds that pride and rebellion lead to bondage, while submission to God alone brings true freedom.

sens: Meeting of people deliberating together
Group of close friends or confidants who share mutual trust
Advice or plan shared with others
Secret entrusted to a few
Wicked plan against someone
Trusting intimacy with God
H5475.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to an assembly, a group gathered to discuss and make decisions: "Plans fail for lack of counsel" (Proverbs 15:22) shows how people come together to deliberate.
2. It also evokes the circle of intimates, close friends who speak to each other in confidence: Job says, "Oh, that I were as in months gone by, as in the days when God watched over me" (Job 29:4), where "friend" translates this word and refers to one with whom intimacy is shared.
3. Counsel is also the advice or plan communicated within this confidential circle: it is the content of what is said among intimates.
4. Often, the word carries the idea of secrecy, of what is not disclosed to the public: "A gossip betrays a confidence" (Proverbs 11:13) shows that one betrays what should remain hidden.
5. In the Psalms, it sometimes designates the plot of the wicked: "Hide me from the secret plots of the wicked" (Psalms 64:3) speaks of a malicious plan concerted in secret.
6. In relation to God, it is the trusting intimacy of the prophet or believer: Jeremiah asks, "Who has stood in the counsel of the Lord?" (Jeremiah 23:18), speaking of the divine mystery revealed to true prophets.
H5475.origine: The Hebrew word sod comes from a root that evokes the idea of sitting together, gathering in a group. It is close to the verb "to sit" or "to converse." The basic image is that of a group of people sitting together, exchanging words in trust — hence the idea of counsel, confidence, and shared secret among close ones. The word carries with it an atmosphere of intimacy and familiarity.
H5475.emploi: This word appears 21 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms, Proverbs, and Jeremiah. It designates sometimes a real assembly ("the assembly of the upright," Psalms 111:1), sometimes a group of close friends (Job 29:4), and sometimes a secret or hidden plan (Proverbs 15:22, Psalms 64:3). In Proverbs, it often speaks of one who reveals or keeps a secret. In Jeremiah, it takes on a prophetic dimension: the true prophet is one who "stands in the counsel of the Lord" (Jeremiah 23:18, 23:22), while false prophets have not listened to it. The nuance varies: official meeting, intimate circle, secret plan, or spiritual intimacy with God.
H5475.portee: This word reminds us that true decisions are made in trust, within a small circle, away from the tumult. For the believer, it invokes the idea of a shared secret with God — not a secret that is hidden, but a trusting intimacy where God confides His will to us. It is also a warning: the secrets of the wicked and their plots are ultimately exposed on the day of God.

sens: Father of Gaddiel, one of the twelve spies sent to explore Canaan
H5476.detail: Sodi is an Israelite man living during the time of the Exodus and the wilderness. He is known only as the father of Gaddiel, who was chosen to represent the tribe of Zebulun among the twelve spies that Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Numbers 13:10).
H5476.origine: The name Sodi means "knowledge" or "confidant" in Hebrew, derived from a root that evokes the idea of "secret" or "intimacy." It is a common Semitic name in Israel.
H5476.emploi: Sodi appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 13:10. He is mentioned only in the list of the twelve spies, where he is identified as the father of Gaddiel. No other information is given about him — his name is listed solely to establish the genealogy and identity of the representative of Zebulun.

sens: Son of Tzophach, from the tribe of Asher
H5477.detail: Suach is a man from the tribe of Asher, living during the time of the Divided Monarchy in Israel. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:36, as one of the sons of the patriarch Tzophach. His name appears in a genealogical enumeration that recaps the descendants of Asher, one of the twelve tribes of Israel.
H5477.origine: The name Suach literally means "who sweeps" or "sweeping," formed from a Hebrew root related to the verb "to sweep." This descriptive name was common in Israel: it evokes an ordinary action, that of sweeping, and may have carried, for the one who first received it, a prophetic or simply familial significance.
H5477.emploi: Suach is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:36. This verse records his name in the genealogy of the sons of Tzophach, himself a son of Asher. The context is purely genealogical: nothing is known about him beyond his belonging to this family and his time, that of the separated kingdoms of Israel and Judah. His appearance in Chronicles shows the importance that the Bible attaches to tribal lineage, even for minor figures.

sens: Waste, garbage that is swept up
Thrown away thing, of no value
Dead bodies treated as waste
H5478.detail:
1. A sweeping is what is collected when sweeping the floor: dust, crumbs, remnants that are pushed aside. It is the refuse, what is not kept and is thrown away (Isaiah 5:25).
2. By extension, it refers to what has no value, what is despised and abandoned without consideration.
3. In the passage from Isaiah, corpses are compared to sweepings: treated like garbage, scattered in the streets without honor or dignity, a testimony to the annihilation of divine judgment.
H5478.origine: The Hebrew word סוּחָה comes from a root that means "to sweep" or "to clean." It evokes the concrete and mundane image of daily sweeping: chasing away debris to clean. The word literally designates what falls under the broom, what is swept and thrown away. It is a word from ordinary language, which sensitively conveys the idea of humiliation and rejection.
H5478.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (Isaiah 5:25). It figures in an image of striking rhetorical power: the prophet denounces the Lord's judgment on Israel. The corpses of the dead are thrown into the streets "like sweepings," tossed haphazardly without ceremony, without a dignified burial. This comparison reinforces the horror of the punishment: not only does death strike, but human dignity is denied, bodies are treated like garbage. It is the lowest image of contempt and destruction.
H5478.portee: This dark word reminds us that God's judgment on sin is real and terrible. It invites the reader to take the prophetic warning seriously and to seek repentance rather than persist in rebellion. The raw image of corpses as sweepings shows that without conversion, only humiliation and death remain.

sens: man of the time of Exile and Return
ancestor of a family of temple servants
H5479.detail: Sothai is a man mentioned at the time of Judah's return from exile to Babylon. He is presented as the ancestor of a family of servants who had served in Solomon's temple. His name appears in the genealogical lists of the descendants of the temple servants who returned from captivity with Zerubbabel, around 538 B.C.
H5479.origine: The name Sothai means "changing" or "unstable" in Hebrew, formed from a root that evokes change. This name is borne by this character during the reconstruction of the temple after the Babylonian Exile.
H5479.emploi: Sothai is mentioned twice in the scriptures: in Ezra 2:55 and Nehemiah 7:57, in almost identical lists enumerating the descendants of Solomon's servants who participated in the return from exile with Zerubbabel. These lists attest that his family survived the Babylonian captivity and was able to return to rebuild the temple. He represents the continuity of temple service through generations, despite the interruption of the Exile.

sens: to apply oil to the skin or hair
to perfume or care for the body with oil
to show respect or honor to someone through anointing
to mark with a holy anointing for a mission or dignity
H5480.detail:
1. Anointing is the act of pouring or applying oil to the body, hair, or skin. This was a daily practice in Israel, especially after washing: Ruth washes and anoints herself before going to see Boaz (Ruth 3:3), and David anoints himself as a sign of returning to normal life after his mourning (2 Samuel 12:20). In times of mourning or calamity, not anointing marked sadness: the woman sent to King David shows her distress by refusing to anoint herself with oil (2 Samuel 14:2).
2. Anointing someone with oil is also a way to show honor and care. When the captives from Samaria were exhausted, they were anointed before being given food and drink (2 Chronicles 28:15) — it was an act of restoration and hospitality. Similarly, God anointed Jerusalem with oil as a sign of purification and care (Ezekiel 16:9).
3. Anointing also carries a spiritual meaning: pouring oil on someone or allowing oneself to be anointed is to receive a blessing, a consecration, or a divine mission. This practice is linked to royalty and the priesthood in Israel.
H5480.origine: The Hebrew verb sukh means to spread, to pour oil. The basic image is that of the act of pouring oil on someone or oneself — a daily gesture in the ancient Near East, where oil was used for hygiene, care, and honor. The word belongs to the same family as the idea of friction and application: anointing is a concrete and visible act. In Hebrew, this root is related to practices of beautification and sanctification of the body.
H5480.emploi: The verb anoint appears 8 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the Qal (simple form) and once in the Hiphil (causative form). The usages are divided among three contexts: hygiene and personal appearance (Ruth 3:3, 2 Samuel 12:20), mourning and its markers (Deuteronomy 28:40, 2 Samuel 14:2), and hospitality or restoration (2 Chronicles 28:15, Ezekiel 16:9). Sometimes the refusal to anoint expresses deep affliction (2 Samuel 14:2, Micah 6:15 mentions the non-use of oil in times of trouble). The word also takes on a spiritual hue: anointing is an act of consecration and divine blessing.
H5480.portee: Anointing in the Bible is never a trivial gesture: it is an act filled with dignity, care, and spirituality. Understanding this word helps the reader see that the Lord does not disdain the simple gestures of beauty, restoration, and honor — those very ones He uses to speak of His tenderness toward His people. It also sheds light on the meaning of anointing in the Christian tradition: to be anointed with the Spirit is to be marked for a mission and restored by grace.

sens: Wind musical instrument, made of pipes and an air bag
Instrument used in royal orchestras for solemn ceremonies
H5481.detail:
1. The bagpipe is a wind musical instrument that produces sound by vibrating air in pipes. It can refer to several types of ancient wind instruments (shawm, double pipe, or panpipes), all capable of producing distinct melodies. In Daniel 3:5, it is among the instruments that Nebuchadnezzar commands to be sounded at the dedication of his golden statue.

2. In the context of the Babylonian king, the bagpipe is not a mere amusement: it is an official instrument that accompanies royal commands and ceremonies of power. Its sound is meant to trigger obedience and worship. This shows how music was used to serve authority and political propaganda: when the bagpipe sounds, it is a signal to obey immediately.
H5481.origine: The Greek word symphônia (from which the French 'symphonie' derives) literally means 'agreement of sounds' or 'harmony'. The bagpipe is an ancient Greek instrument well attested in historical sources. The word points to the idea that multiple pipes produce harmonized sounds together, creating a complex and impressive musical effect.
H5481.emploi: The word appears only four times in the New Testament, all in the book of Daniel in chapter 3. It is included in the official list of instruments that King Nebuchadnezzar commands to be sounded at the dedication of the golden statue: trumpet, shawm, lyre, sambuca, psaltery, bagpipe, and other instruments. Each mention (verses 5, 7, 10, 15) repeats this same enumeration in the context of the royal decree requiring the peoples to bow down and worship the idol. The bagpipe thus embodies the instrument of idolatrous seduction and tyrannical power.
H5481.portee: For the reader, the bagpipe serves as a reminder that idolatry relies on spectacle, music, and emotions to impose obedience. This major instrument of the Babylonian concert represents the persuasive force that idol worship exerts on the masses. But the story of Daniel and his three companions shows that true fidelity to God must remain impervious to these seductions; it is a call to discern, in our own cultures, what seeks to divert us from true worship.

sens: City in Egypt to the south, near the borders of Ethiopia
H5482.detail: Syene is a city located in the southern part of ancient Egypt, near the lands of Ethiopia. It marks the southern limit of Egyptian territory. The two biblical mentions cite it in contrast with Migdol (a fortress in the north), showing that God announces His judgment on Egypt from north to south: 'From Migdol to Syene, they shall fall by the sword' (Ezekiel 30:6).
H5482.origine: The Hebrew name סְוֵנִים (Syenim) or סִינִים (Sinim) designates this ancient Egyptian city, also known as Assouan. It was an important commercial and military center, controlling the passage of the Nile to the south and Ethiopia.
H5482.emploi: Syene appears twice in the book of Ezekiel, in chapters 29 and 30. These two occurrences are announcements of judgment pronounced by the prophet against Egypt. In both cases, Syene represents the southern limit of the country, and it is associated with Migdol (to the north) to signify that divine judgment will extend over all the territory of Egypt, from north to south.
H5482.portee: Mentioning Syene reminds us that God's judgments know no geographical limits: He exercises His authority over all nations, even to the ends of the known earth. For the reader, this reinforces the confidence that nothing escapes the Lord's control, not even the great earthly powers.

sens: migratory bird with pointed wings and fast flight
characteristic cry of this bird
natural instinct and sagacity of creatures
H5483A.detail:
1. The swallow is a small bird known for its very fast flight and agility in the air, with pointed and tapered wings. Isaiah 38:14 shows it "fluttering," highlighting this ability to move quickly and tirelessly in the sky.
2. The word also refers to the characteristic cry that this bird makes — a sharp and repeated sound. It is through this cry that the prophet Isaiah expresses his own anguish: "I cried like a swallow."
3. The swallow represents the natural instinct and sagacity of animals: Jeremiah 8:7 mentions it among other migratory birds that "know in the heavens their season" and "observe the time of their arrival," contrasting the faithfulness of creatures to the divine order with the unfaithfulness of the people of Israel.
H5483A.origine: The Hebrew word sus designates this migratory bird characterized by its fast flight and lively movements. The same word also appears in Aramaic with the same meaning. Its initial image is that of speed and agility, making it a natural symbol of agitation and trouble for those who imitate it.
H5483A.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. It first appears in Isaiah (Isaiah 38:14), where the sick prophet imitates the cry of the swallow to express his spiritual and physical anguish. Then in Jeremiah (Jeremiah 8:7), where the swallow is mentioned with other birds as an example of creatures obeying the natural laws of migration, which makes Israel's inattention to the divine law all the more serious. In both cases, the bird is depicted as a living creature, observed or imitated, never in an abstract manner.
H5483A.portee: These two passages invite the reader to meditate on two realities: on one hand, the depth of suffering and anguish when the cry of the soul becomes like that of a wounded creature; on the other hand, the guilt of Israel, for even wild animals recognize the order that God has established, while the chosen people remain deaf to it. It is a call to return to obedience.

sens: domestic animal for work and riding, used for transport and war
Gate of Jerusalem called the Horse Gate
H5483B.detail:
1. The horse is the noble animal par excellence in the Bible: a powerful and fast draft animal, mount of warriors and kings. It is a prestigious animal, reserved for the great and for military expeditions. Although primarily used here to designate a gate of Jerusalem, the word evokes this value.
2. The Horse Gate was one of the gates of Jerusalem, probably located near the east of the city, not far from the temple. It takes its name from the horse — perhaps because it was through there that royal or military horses passed. Nehemiah mentions it during the reconstruction of the walls (Nehemiah 3:28), and Jeremiah refers to it when he speaks of the consecration of the Valley of Hinnom to the Lord (Jeremiah 31:40).
H5483B.origine: The Hebrew word sus comes from a root that fundamentally means horse, this large and majestic animal, highly valued in the ancient Near East. It is a simple and ancient word, without diminutive: it designates the animal in its nobility. The Horse Gate of Jerusalem bears this name because it was associated with the use of horses, perhaps a place of passage or royal stable.
H5483B.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, but exclusively to designate the Horse Gate of Jerusalem, not the horse itself. Both Nehemiah and Jeremiah mention it in an urban and religious context: Nehemiah during the reconstruction of the walls (Nehemiah 3:28), Jeremiah when he prophesies the consecration of the Valley of Hinnom (Jeremiah 31:40). These two uses indicate that the Horse Gate was a well-known and important entrance to Jerusalem, probably facing east, near the temple area.
H5483B.portee: This word reminds us that the holy city of Jerusalem had named gates, concrete and identified places where the service of God and His people was fulfilled. The mention of the Horse Gate anchors us in the physical reality of the city restored under Nehemiah, and in the prophetic promises of Jeremiah: God also guided through the paths and gates of His people.

sens: draft or riding animal, mounted or harnessed to a chariot or vehicle
war or prestige mount, sign of military power and wealth
image of brute strength, devoid of wisdom or discernment
in figurative language, human resource in which one places trust
H5483M.detail:
1. The horse is primarily a domestic animal that the Bible mentions in various contexts: transporting people, pulling war chariots, commerce, and wealth. Genesis 47:17 shows Joseph accepting horses as payment for grain in Egypt; 1 Kings 18:5 mentions Ahab sending to seek grass to keep his horses alive during a famine.
2. The horse symbolizes military power and royal prestige: kings ride in chariots drawn by horses (Jeremiah 17:25); possessing many horses marks the greatness of a monarch (Solomon had thousands). It is a sign of dominance and strength in war.
3. Despite its vigor, the horse remains a creature without its own reason: Psalm 33:17 declares that "the horse is a vain hope for salvation," for its physical strength cannot create victory without God's help.
4. Figuratively, placing trust in horses means placing trust in human military forces rather than in God. Hosea 14:3 refuses to say: "Our horses will save us," thus renouncing the support of foreign powers to turn to God alone.
H5483M.origine: The Hebrew word sus comes from a root that expresses the idea of "leaping" or "bounding," evoking the rapid pace of the horse at a gallop. This etymology reflects one of the most remarkable qualities of the animal: its speed. In the Old Testament, the horse appears as an exotic animal in Canaan (Egyptian chariots had them), brought in large numbers during conquests and Eastern trade.
H5483M.emploi: The word horse appears 130 times in the Segond, mainly in the historical accounts of the kings of Israel and Judah, the wars against Egypt (the Pharaoh's horses submerged in the Red Sea: Exodus 15), and prophetic oracles. It is also found in wisdom poems where it becomes a moral image. The meaning varies slightly: sometimes it is the physical animal (fed, ridden), sometimes the image of military power (trust in horses = trust in armies), sometimes the expression of a weakness or a wandering of the human heart. The prophets particularly criticize the Assyrian and Egypt who rely on their war chariots rather than on faith in God.
H5483M.portee: The horse in the Bible brings the reader back to the profound question of where to place one's trust. A powerful, fast, and impressive animal, yet incapable of saving — this is a lesson that the prophets address to all who base their security on human means rather than on God. This word invites the believer to discern between visible strength and true divine protection, and not to confuse external power with true help.

sens: Female horse
H5484.detail: 1. A mare is a female horse, a highly valued draft and war animal in the Old Testament. In Song of Solomon 1:9, the lover compares his friend to a mare of Pharaoh's chariots, one of the most beautiful and noble in the known world: it is a compliment on her beauty and presence.
H5484.origine: The Hebrew word סוּסָה (sousah) comes from the root of סוּס (sus, the horse). The mare, as the female of the horse, naturally carries this generic name with a feminine marker. Horses, important for the army and the prestige of kings in the Near East, hold a central place in the biblical imagination.
H5484.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the Song of Solomon. The use of the feminine (mare rather than horse) is not trivial: it emphasizes not only the femininity of the friend but also the elegance and grace of the animal to which she is compared. Compared to Pharaoh's horses, reputed to be the most beautiful and strongest, the friend is placed among the most noble and admirable creatures.
H5484.portee: This verse invites the reader to reflect on beauty seen not as superficial, but as a reflection of inner nobility and quiet strength. Being compared to a mare of Pharaoh is to be recognized as precious, worthy of honor and genuine admiration.

sens: Man living during the time of the Exodus and the desert
H5485.detail: Susi is the father of Gaddi, who was chosen as one of the twelve spies sent by Moses to explore the land of Canaan. Gaddi represented the tribe of Manasseh during this mission recounted in Numbers 13.
H5485.origine: The name Susi means "my horse" in Hebrew, formed from the root sus ("horse"). This name was borne by Hebrews during the Mosaic period, and it evokes an image of strength and speed.
H5485.emploi: Susi appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 13:11, where he is identified as the father of Gaddi. His son Gaddi is one of the twelve men sent by Moses to scout the promised land. Although Susi himself did not play a prominent role in biblical narratives, his name persists in history through his son, one of the representatives of the tribes of Israel.

sens: cease to exist, disappear
come to an end, finish
make disappear, destroy
completely annihilate
H5486.detail:
1. Cease to exist, disappear: the word evokes the idea that something comes to an end, fades from the world. It is the natural or forced end of a reality. In Esther 9:28, the memory of the feast of Purim was never to "be erased" among the descendants of the Jews: the idea is that the memory would persist, that it would not disappear.
2. Come to an end, finish: it is the fulfillment or completion of a period, an action that exhausts itself. In Jeremiah 8:13, the Lord says, "I want to finish with them," which means that judgment will put an end to their existence.
3. Make disappear, destroy: the verb shifts from an intransitive sense ("finish oneself") to an active sense where the speaker causes the end of a reality. In Zephaniah 1:2-3, the Lord declares, "I will destroy everything on the face of the earth" and "I will destroy man and beast": it is the divine action that ends the creatures.
4. Completely annihilate: a maximum level of intensity, where destruction is total and irreversible. In Psalms 73:19, the wicked are suddenly "destroyed," "taken away, annihilated by a sudden end": it is a divine judgment that erases a reality from the world.
H5486.origine: The Hebrew verb suph comes from a root that fundamentally means "come to an end, cease." It is a verb of temporal movement, describing the passage of a reality from existence to non-existence. The same root gives in Aramaic suph with the meaning "to be accomplished, to be fulfilled." The word evokes the image of a race that reaches its end, of a duration that exhausts itself.
H5486.emploi: The verb suph appears 6 times in the provided texts, mainly in the prophets (Zephaniah, Jeremiah, Isaiah) and the Psalms, with a use in Esther. It almost always pertains to a divine judgment or a reality that disappears under God's action. When the subject is human or divine in the active sense (Zephaniah 1:2-3), the verb means "to destroy": God annihilates what exists. When it is intransitive (Esther 9:28, Psalms 73:19), it describes the end of something or the erasure of a memory. The context of eschatological judgment often recurs: it is in the great texts announcing the end of times that this verb emerges with force.
H5486.portee: Meditating on this verb reminds us that all earthly reality has an end: what seems stable and eternal in the eyes of men is mortal and transient for God. The divine judgment announced by the prophets should not terrify the repentant believer, but invite him to base his life on what does not perish. The destruction announced in Zephaniah invites us to consider the gravity of sin and the certainty of God's judgment, but also the hope for those who turn to Him.

sens: Bring something to its conclusion, give it its end
Make disappear, annihilate, completely destroy
H5487.detail:
1. To accomplish means to carry out an action or process to its completion: it is to finish, complete what was underway. In Daniel 4:33, the prophetic word "is fulfilled on Nebuchadnezzar" — the prediction is fully realized, the announced events come to their end.
2. To annihilate is to cause something to cease to exist, to destroy it entirely. In Daniel 2:44, the God of heaven "will annihilate all these kingdoms": these empires will completely disappear, reduced to nothing by divine power.
H5487.origine: The Hebrew verb suph comes from a root that evokes the idea of end, completion, and disappearance. The same root appears in other biblical contexts to express the fulfillment of a word or total destruction. The basic image is that of an action carried out to the end, or of something that ceases to exist.
H5487.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the provided Hebrew biblical text, both in the book of Daniel, which reports the words and visions of the prophet at the court of Babylon. In Daniel 2:44, it refers to the final destruction of earthly kingdoms by the eternal kingdom of God. In Daniel 4:33, the same verb describes the fulfillment of the divine sentence pronounced against King Nebuchadnezzar: his punishment becomes real, it is executed. The word thus shifts from the meaning "to destroy" (the kingdoms) to the meaning "to fully realize" (the prediction).
H5487.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that God's words never remain suspended: they are always fulfilled. It also shows that divine judgment on the powers of the world is certain and complete — no human empire survives against the eternal reign of the Lord. It is a source of confidence in divine faithfulness.

sens: vast expanse of salt water between Africa and Arabia
site of the miraculous crossing of the Hebrews fleeing Egypt
boundary and limit of the territory promised to Israel
symbol of God's saving power
H5488G.detail: 1. The Red Sea is the vast body of water that stretches between Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, including the Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Aqaba (1 Kings 9:26: Solomon built ships there at Ezion-geber). 2. It is especially famous as the place where the Lord performed the miracle of the crossing: by dividing its waters, He allowed the Hebrews to cross on dry ground while the Egyptian army drowned (Exodus 15:4: "He threw Pharaoh's chariots and his army into the sea"). 3. It marks a natural boundary of the territory that God promised to Israel: from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean (Exodus 23:31: "I will set your borders from the Red Sea to the Sea of the Philistines"). 4. In Israel's memory, this place becomes a symbol of salvation and divine protection: the people remember the "wonders at the Red Sea" and recognize God's hand (Psalms 106:22).
H5488G.origine: The Hebrew name suph (סוּף), "red," describes the characteristic color of this sea, likely due to the red rocks that border it or the mineral particles suspended in its waters. In Greek, the translators of the Old Testament rendered it as eruthros ("Red Sea"), although some ancient manuscripts refer to it as "Sea of Reeds" (thalassa kalámou), which may reflect a different reading of biblical geography. The Hebrew word suph thus becomes a fundamental geographical and theological landmark.
H5488G.emploi: Suph appears 24 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the Pentateuch (Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) and in the accounts of the conquest (Joshua, Judges). It is first mentioned during the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 10:19: the locusts are hurled there), then at the time of the miraculous crossing (Exodus 15:4 and following), and subsequently throughout the desert, marking the stages of the journey (Numbers 33:10-11). In the Psalms, it returns as a memorial of divine wonders (Psalms 106, 136). Its usage changes little: it is always the same place, both geographically and theologically.
H5488G.portee: The Red Sea is much more than a barrier of water: it is the theater where God dramatically and irrevocably saved His people. For the believer, it reminds us that the Lord never abandons His people to the hands of their enemies, even when all seems lost. It also invites us to recognize that God sets boundaries and limits, not to imprison, but to protect and guide. Each mention of the Red Sea in the Bible rekindles faith: God acted, God acts, God will act.

sens: Aquatic plant with straight, flexible stems that grows by the water's edge
That which surrounds or encircles, in a figurative sense
H5488H.detail:
1. The reed is a plant that grows in or near water, with thin and flexible stems. It is a well-known image in Egypt: Moses' mother places the child in a basket and hides it among the reeds of the Nile (Exodus 2:3), where the shallow water offers refuge and camouflage. When the rivers of Egypt dry up, it is a sign of disaster: "The reeds and rushes will wither" (Isaiah 19:6), for this plant depends entirely on water.
2. Figuratively, reeds can evoke that which envelops or seizes: Jonah, engulfed by the abyss, says, "The reeds wrapped around my head" (Jonah 2:6), describing his feeling of being overwhelmed and suffocated by the waters of death.
H5488H.origine: The Hebrew word סוּף (suph) literally designates the reeds that abound in Egypt and along the waters of the Middle East. It belongs to the same family as the expression "Sea of Reeds" (yam suph), which refers to the Red Sea — probably because its shores or shallow reefs were covered with reeds. The word evokes the simple and tangible image of a fragile, flexible plant that bends in the breeze.
H5488H.emploi: The word appears four times in the Segond, always in the literal sense of aquatic plant. Three occurrences concern Egypt: the Nile where Moses is hidden (Exodus 2:3 and 2:5, twice) and the rivers that dry up during the plagues (Isaiah 19:6). Only one uses it in a more figurative sense: Jonah, in the belly of the fish, feeling the reeds surround him (Jonah 2:6). The context is always dramatic or miraculous: rescue, judgment, or absolute distress.
H5488H.portee: The reed reminds us that God saves His people even in the most humble and hidden places: Moses, abandoned, is preserved among the reeds of Egypt. It is also an image of fragility — reeds break and wither — which contrasts with the strength of the One who protects us through the waters.

sens: Place or region in the desert of Arabia, east of the Jordan
H5489.detail: Suph is a geographical site located in the desert, mentioned only once in the Bible as a landmark to locate the place where Moses delivers his speeches to Israel. It is a place that lies across the Jordan, in the desert plain, near other places named Paran, Tophel, and Laban (Deuteronomy 1:1).
H5489.origine: The name Suph comes from Hebrew and literally means "seaweed" or "kelp" — the grass of the sea. It is a term that usually designates marine vegetation, suggesting that this place may have a historical link to a wetland or marsh in the desert, although its precise geographical location today remains uncertain.
H5489.emploi: Suph appears only once in the Bible, in Deuteronomy 1:1, where it is listed among the geographical landmarks used to situate Moses' speech to Israel before entering the Promised Land. It is a proper name of a place in the desert of Arabia, used solely to establish the historical and geographical context of the transmission of the Law.

sens: The ultimate point or extreme limit in space
The moment when something comes to an end in time
The culmination or ultimate consequence of an action
Death or the final destiny of man
The conclusion of a speech or narrative
H5490.detail:
1. The ultimate point or extreme limit in space: this is the place where something stops, its spatial limit. In 2 Chronicles 20:16, Jehoshaphat must find the enemy "at the end of the valley," meaning at its end, where the valley finishes.
2. The moment when something comes to an end in time: this is the last stage of a process, when a period concludes. In Ecclesiastes 3:11, "from the beginning to the end" describes the entirety of the time that a work occupies, from start to finish.
3. The culmination or ultimate consequence of an action: this is what everything converges toward. In Ecclesiastes 7:2, "the end of all man" means that death is the inevitable common destiny toward which everyone tends.
4. Death or the final destiny of man: this is the ultimate moment of life, the passage that no one escapes. The passage shows that this final term concentrates the meaning of the entire life.
5. The conclusion of a speech or narrative: this is the last part, what comes last. In Ecclesiastes 12:15, "the end of the speech" refers to the ultimate words that summarize and crown all that precedes it.
H5490.origine: The Hebrew word soph comes from a root expressing the idea of stopping or limit. It describes what interrupts, what naturally comes to an end. The word evokes the image of the end of a rope, the last stone of a wall, the last drop of water. It is a simple and ancient word, common in the Hebrew language to speak of any form of conclusion or extremity.
H5490.emploi: The word soph appears 5 times in the provided usages, spread across Chronicles, Ecclesiastes, and Joel. In 2 Chronicles 20:16, it designates the geographical end of a valley. Ecclesiastes, with its 3 occurrences, uses it in a deeper and meditative way: the end of time and the completion of works (3:11), death as a universal destiny (7:2), and the conclusion of teachings (12:15). In Joel 2:20, the rear guard of an army represents the end of a troop. The word thus oscillates between the spatial (end of a valley, rear of an army) and the temporal (end of life, end of a message).
H5490.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on what comes to an end and what lasts. Ecclesiastes uses it to awaken awareness: knowing that every man has an end, that everything has its term, gives weight to daily choices. Recognizing that God knows the end of all things—from the beginning to the end—strengthens the confidence that our life is part of a divine plan.

sens: The extremity of an object or space, its ultimate edge
The conclusion, the completion of something that comes to an end
The culmination, that toward which a reality or situation tends
The future eternity, the end of times
The absolute or the absence of limit (in negative expressions)
H5491.detail:
1. The extremity of an object or space: the point to which something physical extends. In Daniel 4:11 and 4:22, the enormous tree rises to the heavens and is seen "from the ends of the whole earth"—this refers to the edges, the farthest limits of the inhabited earth.

2. The conclusion, the completion: when something comes to an end, reaches its term. In Daniel 7:28, the words of the vision "ended"—they stopped there, they had a final point.

3. The culmination of a situation: the destiny toward which a reality tends. The dominion of the king "will never be destroyed" (Daniel 6:26) means that it will have no end, that no term will come to annihilate it.

4. The future eternity or definitive absence: when it is said that a power will be destroyed "forever" (Daniel 7:26), it speaks of the moment when it will come to an end forever, where no return will be possible—a final and absolute end.

5. The idea is often one of permanence or limit: in these Aramaic texts, "end" evokes both the geographical end of a land and the ultimate term of a dominion or the eternity of a reign.
H5491.origine: This Aramaic word סוֹף (soph) is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew word סוֹף (soph) of number H5490 ("end"). It shares a root that evokes the idea of encircling, limiting, or closing something, as one would close a loop or a limit. In Aramaic, used mainly in the book of Daniel, it expresses both the spatial edge of a region and the temporal term of a reality—this moment or place where something "stops." The family of the word includes the general idea of culmination and limit.
H5491.emploi: סוֹף appears 5 times in the Aramaic New Testament (that is, the book of Daniel), always with nuances related to completion or limit. In Daniel 4:11-4:22, it designates the geographical extremity, the limits of the earth from which the tree of the dream is seen. In Daniel 6:26, it characterizes the eternity of God's reign, which lasts "until the end" of the ages, that is, without end. In Daniel 7:26-7:28, it first marks the definitive destruction of the power of the wicked king ("forever"), then the completion of the vision itself ("the words ended"). Each time, the word expresses a limit, a culmination, or an eternal permanence.
H5491.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds that all earthly power has an end—even the greatest human reigns will one day be destroyed and annihilated. Conversely, the kingdom of God knows no end: it lasts "until the end," that is, eternally. This promise comforts the believer in the face of hostile powers of his time: what seems invincible here will have a term, while God's dominion is perpetual. The word invites one to place their hope not in present realities, but in what lasts without end.

sens: Violent movement of air that spins on itself
Storm, tempest, destructive wind
Image of God's judgment that sweeps away the wicked
Speed and power of an army or chariot
H5492A.detail:
1. The whirlwind is a natural phenomenon: a wind that turns with force, like in a cyclone or tornado. Job 21:18 mentions that the wicked are "swept away by the wind, like chaff carried away by the whirlwind"—an image of lightness and dispersion.
2. More broadly, the word designates a furious storm, a devastating tempest. In Isaiah 21:1, "the whirlwind of the south" advances like an irresistible force coming from the desert.
3. In biblical language, God uses the whirlwind as an image of His judgment: in Proverbs 1:27, He falls upon the wicked "like a storm," and in Isaiah 66:15, the Lord comes "in a whirlwind" of fire and anger to punish.
4. The word also describes speed and overwhelming power: in Isaiah 5:28, the wheels of war chariots resemble a whirlwind—a symbol of an irresistible and destructive advance.
H5492A.origine: The Hebrew word sopah comes from a root that evokes turbulent and violent movement. It is related to other Hebrew words designating movement, whirlwind, or storm. The central image is that of a natural force that spins, sweeping everything in its path—hence its use to describe both meteorological phenomena and divine anger or military power.
H5492A.emploi: The word appears 15 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the poetic books (Job, Psalms, Proverbs) and the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hosea, Amos, Nahum). It primarily designates natural phenomena: storms and destructive winds. But gradually, the biblical text makes it an image of divine judgment—God "rides the whirlwind" to chastise the wicked. It also becomes a military image: the arrival of an army resembles a whirlwind that devastates everything. The context transforms the word: concrete when it concerns nature, metaphorical when it expresses the power of God or of war.
H5492A.portee: For the believer, this word reminds that God does not remain indifferent to evil: He intervenes with the power of an inevitable storm. It also invites trust: the righteous will not be swept away like chaff. Finally, it teaches humility before the divine omnipotence—a force that no one can stop, except by turning to Him.

sens: Place in Transjordan mentioned in an ancient war song
H5492B.detail: Supha is a location situated east of the Jordan, in Transjordan. It appears only once in the Bible, cited in a poetic formula from the "Book of the Wars of the Lord" (Numbers 21:14), an ancient collection of Israelite military songs. The context refers to the campaigns of Moses and the Israelites during the conquest of the territory east of the Jordan, alongside other places like Waheb and the torrents of Arnon. It is a fragment of war poetry that bears witness to the history of the battles fought by Israel.
H5492B.origine: The name Supha comes from a Hebrew root meaning "overflow" or "streaming," which evokes a watercourse or a place marked by water. This etymology aligns with the context of Numbers 21:14, where Supha is mentioned alongside torrents and significant watercourses of the Transjordan region.
H5492B.emploi: Supha appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 21:14. It is cited in a verse that reproduces an excerpt from the "Book of the Wars of the Lord," an ancient document to which Scripture refers to document Israel's military victories before settling in Canaan. This unique mention shows that Supha was a geographical landmark known to the Israelites, likely a strategic location marking campaigns against the Amorite kings and other neighboring peoples.

sens: To take something away from its place
To leave a place, to go away, to withdraw
To put an end to something, to make it disappear
To refuse, to take back a possession or favor
To take away a burden, an affliction, a curse
H5493G.detail:
1. To take something away from its place — the most concrete meaning: to physically remove an object. Noah "removed" the covering of the ark to see if the land was dry (Genesis 8:13); Joseph "removed" from his hand the ring of Pharaoh to give it back to the king (Genesis 41:42).
2. To leave a place, to go away, to withdraw — to withdraw oneself from a location or situation. The cloud of divine presence "withdrew" from the tent of meeting when Miriam was struck with leprosy (Numbers 12:10); Joab "withdrew" from King Absalom, refusing to obey him (2 Samuel 16:9).
3. To put an end to something, to make it disappear — to interrupt, annul, or destroy. The Lord "removed" Judah from His presence because of the sins of Manasseh (2 Kings 24:3); removing idols and statues was to abolish the worship of false gods (Isaiah 27:9).
4. To refuse, to take back a possession or favor — to cease granting. Job cries that God "refuses" him justice (Job 27:2); God promised that His grace would not be taken away from the Messiah as it had been taken from Saul (2 Samuel 7:15).
5. To take away a burden, an affliction, a curse — to relieve and liberate. The Lord was to "remove" the diseases of Egypt from Israel (Deuteronomy 7:15); God commanded to remove the sin from the people (Joshua 7:13).
H5493G.origine: The Hebrew root סוּר (sur) evokes the idea of turning away, taking another direction. The verb could be reinforced by other grammatical forms to emphasize: "to take aside," "to put at a distance." This notion of diversion or deviation is at the heart of the word: physically, one removes something; morally or spiritually, one turns away from evil or sin; pastorally, God "removes" or "holds back" what He deems good.
H5493G.emploi: The verb סוּר appears 139 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is very frequent in the narratives of the Pentateuch and the Historical Books, and it is also abundant in the description of the religious reforms of the kings of Judah (removal of altars and idols). It is found in various contexts such as: removing a covering (very concrete meaning), withdrawing from a place, removing a curse or sin (moral and spiritual meaning), and refusing or taking back a divine favor. The verb does not change much in fundamental meaning: it always describes a movement of deviation or separation, but its object varies: inanimate object, person, abstract (curse, grace, sin).
H5493G.portee: This word invites the reader to understand how God governs by acting — sometimes by removing what is impure or evil (idols, sins, afflictions), and sometimes by withdrawing His grace or favor in judgment. For the believer, it reminds us that the act of removing or taking away can be liberating (relief from wounds, forgiveness of sin) or threatening (withdrawal of grace). Praying to God to remove sins (Joshua 7:13) is to ask for purity and restored communion.

sens: To turn aside, to leave a direction or path
To move away from a place, to go away
To abandon someone or something
To cease doing something
To remove, to take away, to eliminate
To come to an end, to disappear
H5493H.detail:
1. To turn away means to change direction, to turn back or take another path: one leaves the road one was following (Proverbs 4:27 "Turn not to the right hand nor to the left," meaning do not deviate either way).
2. To move away means to depart far from a place or person: the Israelites leave their tents and do not return home (Judges 20:8 "None of us will go to his tent, and none will return to his house").
3. To abandon someone means to leave them, to forsake them, often in the sense of renouncing or rejecting them: Saul was abandoned by the Spirit of God (1 Samuel 16:14 "The Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul").
4. To cease an action means to stop continuing it: to continue in evil (2 Kings 13:2 "He did not turn away from it," he did not cease doing evil) or to turn away from good by no longer pursuing it.
5. To remove or take away means to eliminate, to take away something or someone: the scepter shall not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10), meaning it shall not be taken away, it shall not be removed.
6. To disappear or come to an end means to cease to exist or subsist: when an impiety is removed, it does not return.
H5493H.origine: This verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of turning or turning away. In Hebrew, it belongs to the family of words related to movement and change of direction. The verb can be conjugated in several ways (simple or causative forms): in the simple form, it emphasizes the personal movement of the one who turns away; in the causative form (to cause to turn away), it is someone else who provokes the turning away, removal, or rejection. The fundamental image is that of a path: one exits it, one leaves it, one goes away.
H5493H.emploi: This verb appears 66 times in the Old Testament, especially in the wisdom books (Proverbs, Psalms) and in the history of Israel (Kings, Chronicles). It expresses the central religious idea: to turn away from evil and sin, or conversely to persist in evil. The kings of Israel "did not turn away" from the idolatry of Jeroboam (2 Kings 13:2, 13:6, 14:24). In Proverbs, the wise are constantly urged to "turn away from evil" (Proverbs 3:7, 13:14), just as the foolish are invited to listen to the path of life. The word also describes God's interventions that "remove" anger, "withdraw" His love, or "take away" a burden.
H5493H.portee: This verb invites us to a constant moral decision: to turn away from evil is to actively choose to abandon it, to reject it, to change from it. It is also to recognize that only God can "remove" us from sin and condemnation. For the believer, it is a call to break with sin and to remain faithful to the path of the Lord.

sens: To turn to the side, to deviate from a direction
To stray from a path, a road, a place
To renounce, abandon a behavior or obedience
To remove, take away physically
To cease, come to an end
To divert someone from a way, to make them deviate
H5493I.detail:
1. To turn to the side, to deviate from a direction: the most direct physical movement of the word, changing trajectory or course. In Genesis 19:2, the angels say they will "enter" Lot's house, which implies turning aside from the street to enter a home.
2. To stray from a path, a road, a place: voluntarily abandoning the path one was following. In Judges 19:11, the servant suggests to "head toward" the city of Jebus, meaning to deviate from the initial route.
3. To renounce, abandon a behavior or obedience: no longer following a moral or religious path. In Deuteronomy 17:17, the king must not "turn aside" in his heart—meaning, he must not abandon faithfulness to God.
4. To remove, take away physically: to take something away from where it was. In 1 Samuel 6:3, it is necessary to "remove" guilt by returning the ark.
5. To cease, come to an end: to reach its term, to disappear. In 2 Chronicles 20:10, Israel "turned aside" from them—the king did not allow Israel to confront them.
6. To divert someone from a way, to make them deviate: causing another to turn aside. In Deuteronomy 11:28, following other gods is to turn aside from the path established by the Lord.
H5493I.origine: The root סור (sur) expresses the fundamental idea of "to turn" or "to deviate," with a clear kinetic image: changing direction. The word can function in the simple voice ("I turn aside"), in the iterative voice ("I continually turn aside"), or in the causative voice ("I cause to turn aside"). This root is common in the Old Testament to describe both physical movement and spiritual movement—turning away from God is literally "to deviate" from His path.
H5493I.emploi: The verb סור appears 81 times in the Old Testament, especially in Deuteronomy, 1 and 2 Samuel, 2 Chronicles, and in the wisdom and prophetic books. Physically, it describes leaving a road or place (Judges 19:11, Genesis 19:2). Morally and spiritually—its most frequent use—it means "to deviate" from God's law, His commandments, or His ways (Deuteronomy 17:17, 28:14; Joshua 1:7; 2 Chronicles 34:2). The book of Job uses it to describe the abandonment of evil (Job 1:1, 1:8: Job "turns aside from evil"). The Psalms and the prophets use it to express the unfaithfulness of the people or their return (Psalms 14:3; Jeremiah 5:23). In the causative voice (Hiphil), it means "to remove," "to take away," "to abolish" (1 Samuel 6:3; 2 Kings 10:29).
H5493I.portee: This word reminds the believer that obeying God means walking straight in His ways without being diverted—an image that speaks to both the feet and the spirit. The opposite notion—"not to turn aside"—becomes a promise: the one who remains attached to the Lord remains safe and blessed (Joshua 1:7, 2 Chronicles 34:2). It is a key biblical term for faithfulness: not deviating means remaining in a right relationship with God and receiving His protection. The opposite, "to turn aside," exposes one to judgment.

sens: to abandon the right path to go elsewhere
to deny or leave the one whom one was to follow
to degenerate, to become unfaithful
H5494.detail:
1. The word describes the action of turning one's back, deviating from a way, a direction, or a person. In Jeremiah 17:13, those who "turn away" from God abandon the source of living water: the image is that of a traveler who leaves the path to get lost in the desert.
2. The word also expresses betrayal or a breach of covenant: it is to deny the one being followed. In Jeremiah 2:21, God reproaches Israel for becoming "a degenerate vine"—the once faithful people have turned away from their God and lost their nature.
3. This turning away leads to degeneration, moral corruption: the one who abandons God does not return unchanged; they become corrupted, they rot internally like spoiled fruit.
H5494.origine: The root evokes the idea of turning, of turning away, of deviating. The word belongs to the semantic field of movement and change of orientation. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it often expresses Israel's unfaithfulness to its covenant with God—a rupture of relationship, not just a physical displacement.
H5494.emploi: The word appears twice in the provided passages, both in Jeremiah, a book where the prophet denounces the unfaithfulness of the people. In Jeremiah 17:13, it qualifies those who abandon God and suffer condemnation. In Jeremiah 2:21, it describes the vine of Israel become degenerate, unfaithful to its Master. The biblical usage focuses on the religious and moral domain: to turn away from God is to deny the covenant and suffer the consequences.
H5494.portee: This word invites the believer to be aware of the danger of unfaithfulness. To stray from God is to stray from the very source of life; it is a progressive degeneration that corrupts the heart. Jeremiah warns: the one who turns away from God to follow other paths finds only confusion and condemnation. For the Christian, it is a call to persevere in faith and not to return to old ways.

sens: Gate of the temple in Jerusalem
H5495.detail: 1. Sur is the name of a gate of the temple in Jerusalem, mentioned in the context of guarding the sacred building. In 2 Kings 11:6, during the protection of the young king Joash, a third of the guards was stationed at this gate, alongside other named gates (the one behind the runners) to ensure the temple's security.
H5495.origine: The name "Sur" literally means "turning aside" or "deviation" in Hebrew, probably referring to a detour or deviation from the normal path. The name may evoke a gate located off to the side or on a side path of the temple.
H5495.emploi: Sur appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 11:6. It is during the reign of King Joash, when the priest Jehoiada organizes the security of the temple to protect the young king. The gate of Sur is listed among the strategic points that the guards must watch to prevent any intrusion.

sens: To push someone to act, to incite them to do something
To attract someone through seduction or deception
To divert someone from their duty or faithfulness
To instigate a wicked or dangerous action
H5496.detail:
1. To push someone to act, to incite them to do something: this means to influence someone to take an action, often a request or deed. When the young wife of Joshua 15:18 solicits her husband, she excites him to ask for a field from his father — she pushes him to act in her favor.

2. To attract someone through seduction or deception: this means to seduce or deceive someone to lead them into a trap or away from the truth. Sennacherib in 2 Chronicles 32:15 seeks to seduce the people by deceiving them about the power of pagan gods.

3. To divert someone from their duty or faithfulness: this means to push them to abandon what they should do or respect. David in 1 Samuel 26:19 fears that someone will excite him against the king, meaning push him to betray his oath.

4. To instigate a wicked or dangerous action: this means to lead someone to commit evil. Jezebel excited Ahab to do evil (1 Kings 21:25), and Satan excited David to count the people (1 Chronicles 21:1) — in both cases, it is pushing towards disobedience.
H5496.origine: The Hebrew verb סוּת comes from a root that fundamentally means "to push" or "to incite." The word belongs to the family of action and movement verbs. It is a verb that emphasizes the influence one person has over another to make them act — whether they are pushed towards good or evil. The form used here (the Hiphil) intensifies this meaning: the speaker does not merely make a suggestion, they truly activate someone to act.
H5496.emploi: The verb סוּת appears 18 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and in the laws (Deuteronomy). It often describes how one person pushes another — sometimes for good (Joshua 15:18, a wife asking her husband), but most often for evil. Ahab is excited by Jezebel, David by Satan, the people by false prophets. The context is very often that of temptation, seduction, or insurrection. The word can also mean "to divert" or "to lead away" (2 Chronicles 18:31, 32:15), always maintaining the idea of an influence that changes someone's direction or will. It is a word of spiritual warfare: it shows how the powers of evil work to divert God's people.
H5496.portee: This word reminds the reader that we are all exposed to influences that push us towards good or evil — whether by other men or by spiritual powers. It invites us to discern who or what excites us, and to resist the seductions that lead us away from faithfulness to God. It is a useful word for understanding how sin reaches us: rarely through brute force, but often through incitement and seduction.

sens: A loose garment that covers the shoulders and back
A prestigious garment, a mark of status or dignity
That which envelops, that which covers
H5497.detail:
1. The mantle is a wide and loose garment worn over other clothes for protection or dignified covering. It is a piece of fabric that covers the shoulders and descends over the back and arms. In Genesis 49:11, Judah's son washes his mantle in wine — a poetic image of extraordinary wealth and abundance.
2. The mantle is also a garment of prestige, worn by one who enjoys power or prosperity. It is not an ordinary garment, but one that is donned to be seen and respected. The image of the mantle stained with wine symbolizes such abundant wealth that one even soils their finest clothes.
3. Figuratively, the mantle refers to that which envelops, that which covers something, like an outer layer that protects and conceals.
H5497.origine: The Hebrew word סוּת (sut) primarily designates a loose garment, close to our French words "soutane" or the Latin "stola." It belongs to the family of Hebrew words that denote outer garments, distinct from tunics and robes worn directly on the skin. The basic image is that of enveloping, covering.
H5497.emploi: The word סוּת appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Genesis 49:11, where Jacob blesses his son Judah. It describes the mantle that Judah washes in wine — a poetic image of extreme fertility and wealth. The context suggests a precious garment, worthy of mention alongside magnificent details: a donkey tied to the vine, wine in abundance. It is a hapax, meaning a word that appears only once in the Hebrew text of the Bible.
H5497.portee: This image of the mantle washed in wine shows us how divine blessing manifests concretely in the believer's life: through abundance, fertility, and prosperity. It invites the reader to envision a wealth so generous that it "stains" even what one possesses that is most beautiful. For the people of Judah, heirs of this blessing, it is the assurance that God thinks of them with overflowing generosity.

sens: To pull something or someone behind oneself on the ground
To drag or carry away by force
To treat with contempt by dragging away from dignity
H5498.detail:
1. To drag primarily means to pull something in a way that makes it slide on the ground. In 2 Samuel 17:13, it speaks of dragging an entire city to the torrent with ropes: the image is that of a mass being pulled for destruction.
2. The word also denotes the action of pulling someone with force, often against their will. In Jeremiah 15:3, dogs drag the corpses of the dead; in Jeremiah 49:20, enemies drag the inhabitants as one drags a flock of weak sheep.
3. To drag also carries the idea of humiliation: in Jeremiah 22:19, the king receives the burial of a donkey, he is dragged and thrown out. It is the ultimate contempt towards a man.
H5498.origine: The Hebrew root is simple and vibrant: it expresses the physical action of pulling, of making slide. It is mainly used in contexts of violence or devastation, never for an ordinary or delicate gesture.
H5498.emploi: This verb appears only 5 times in biblical Hebrew, always in dramatic scenes: destruction of cities, executions, treatment of corpses, or punishments inflicted on enemies. It always involves brute force, exercised on an inert object or on a defenseless being. The contexts are dark: war, divine judgment, death.
H5498.portee: To drag reveals the violence of biblical judgment and the humiliation that awaits the wicked. It is a word that shows that God does not leave crimes and rebellions unpunished. The reader measures the gravity: to be dragged is to lose all honor and dignity. For the believer, it is a call to fear the Lord and not to oppose His will.

sens: piece of fabric torn or worn out by time
rag or tattered cloth that has lost its usefulness
H5499.detail:
1. The word refers to a piece of fabric or cloth that has become too old, too worn, or too damaged to serve its usual purpose. It is a remnant, a waste: something that has been dragged, torn, that has lost its shape and solidity. In Jeremiah 38:11, Ebed-Melech takes worn rags from the king's house, probably scraps, to make soft ropes to lift Jeremiah out of the cistern where he was imprisoned.
2. The image is that of a fabric that has been dragged (the Hebrew word suggests something that is dragged), become so fragile that it can no longer protect or clothe someone decently. These are the rags of the poor or the remnants of a house. In Jeremiah 38:12, Jeremiah must put these worn rags under his armpits so that the ropes do not hurt his skin as he is lifted up.
H5499.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to drag, to pull" — like dragging a rag on the ground. It thus designates what has been dragged, worn, torn by time and use. It is a concrete, rustic word: one who drags their worn belongings, who wears their clothing until they are left with only rags.
H5499.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the same passage (Jeremiah 38:11 and 38:12), during the rescue of Jeremiah by Ebed-Melech. In these two verses, it refers to the textile scraps that Ebed-Melech gathers to protect Jeremiah from the ropes that will lift him out of the cistern. It is a detail of the narrative that shows Ebed-Melech's compassion for the prophet: he even takes care to soften his rescue by protecting his skin.
H5499.portee: This small word reveals God's tenderness towards His servants. Ebed-Melech, a foreigner, risks his life for the prophet and, in addition to saving him, thinks to protect him from injury. The worn rags, the waste, become the instrument of mercy. This teaches that God sees and rewards every act of kindness, even the humblest.
